books.title: Muslims in the Philippines
books.summary: The standard history of the Muslim peoples of the Philippines: the coming of Islam, the sultanates of Sulu and Maguindanao, and three centuries of Spanish wars against them, told from the Moro side of the record. Reissued by the University of the Philippines Press in 1999.
books.overview:
Cesar Adib Majul's history follows the Muslim peoples of the Philippines from the coming of Islam in the 15th century. It traces the growth of Muslim political institutions and the sultanates of mainland Mindanao and Sulu. A large part of the book covers the long wars with Spain, from 1565 to the end of Spanish rule, told as a defence of faith and homeland.

Majul taught at the University of the Philippines from 1948. He wrote the original preface in 1970, and the book came out in 1973 for the university's Asian Center, with maps, a glossary and a bibliography. Reviewers noted his use of sources from outside the Philippines and his treatment of the Sabah claim.

books.title: The Contemporary Muslim Movement in the Philippines
books.summary: Majul’s short account of the Moro struggle of the 1970s and the rise of the Moro National Liberation Front, written for readers abroad.
books.overview:
Cesar Adib Majul's short book on the Muslim movement in the Philippines was published in 1985 by Mizan Press in Berkeley, California. It runs to 162 pages, with notes, a bibliography and an index.

A library record describes it as laying out the political, geographical and historical background needed to understand the movement, for both scholars and general readers. Majul was educated in the Philippines and at Cornell University and taught at the University of the Philippines for most of his career. A biographical profile notes that he played a part in the peace talks between the government and the Moro National Liberation Front.

books.title: Studies in Moro History, Law, and Religion
books.summary: The first English account of Maguindanao’s genealogies and of the law codes and Islam of Maguindanao and Sulu, translated by an American colonial official who read the originals. Out of copyright and free to read.
books.overview:
Najeeb Saleeby's papers were published in 1905 by the Ethnological Survey in Manila, under the American colonial government. They are original studies and translations from Moro texts. Saleeby explains that the tarsila, the written genealogies kept by each sultanate and datuship, were the only written source on early Moro history, and that the datus had long kept them from outsiders. He obtained exact copies from the chief datus of the Rio Grande valley and published their translations for the first time.

The book has 3 chapters. The first covers the history of Magindanao: a sketch of the main Moro settlements, Mindanao mythology, and 8 translated manuscripts. These include the coming of Sharif Kabungsuwan and the conversion of Magindanao to Islam, and the genealogies of Buayan, Bagumbayan and the Iranun datus. The second covers Moro law: a translation of the Luwaran, the Magindanao code, with its Arabic marginal quotations, and 2 Sulu codes. The third gives 2 Sulu orations, one of them a Friday sermon.

books.title: The History of Sulu
books.summary: Sulu from its earliest written genealogies to the American arrival, drawn from the sultanate’s own documents, Spanish records and the author’s years in Jolo. Out of copyright and free to read.
books.overview:
Najeeb M. Saleeby wrote this history for the Division of Ethnology in Manila, and it appeared in 1908. He first went looking for the Genealogy of Sulu, the tarsila, to learn what happened in Sulu before the Spanish came. He writes that it took 2 and a half years, and trips in small Moro boats to visit datus, before the prime minister of the Sultan of Sulu gave him the original manuscript. He also obtained the Annals of Sulu and interviewed leading Tausug elders.

The book opens with a geography of the archipelago and the town of Jolo, then gives a translation of the genealogy. Chapters follow on the coming of Islam and the rise of the sultanate, the long wars with Spain, the treaties of 1836, 1851 and 1878 with translations of their Sulu texts, the decline of Sulu and the reigns of its last sultans up to Jamalul Kiram II.

For the Spanish period Saleeby relied mainly on Colonel Miguel Espina's notes on Jolo. A closing chapter weighs the mistakes of Spanish rule, and appendices reprint Spanish reports and letters.

books.title: Mandate in Moroland
books.subtitle: The American Government of Muslim Filipinos, 1899–1920
books.summary: How the United States ruled the Moro Province and the Department of Mindanao and Sulu, from the Bates Treaty to the start of Filipinization, from the records of the men who governed. Reprinted by New Day in 1983.
books.overview:
This book describes and judges American rule over the Muslims of Mindanao and Sulu from 1899 to 1920. It runs from the first military government, through the Moro Province under Leonard Wood, Tasker Bliss and John Pershing, to Frank Carpenter's civil Department of Mindanao and Sulu from 1914 to 1920. It covers the military, administrative, educational and social sides of American policy and compares it with Spanish policy.

Peter Gowing was an American who joined the faculty of Silliman University in 1960. The book revises his doctoral thesis at Syracuse University and draws on records in the Library of Congress and the US National Archives.

In his foreword, Cesar Adib Majul sums up its main conclusion: the Americans did not fulfil their mandate. The Moros were not prepared to govern themselves when Christian Filipinos took over the Muslim provinces in 1920, and distrust between Muslims and Christians remained.

books.title: Muslim Filipinos: Heritage and Horizon
books.summary: A general introduction to the Muslim peoples of the Philippines, their history, faith and institutions and their place in the republic, written for Filipino readers from the Dansalan Research Center in Marawi.
books.overview:
Peter G. Gowing's book gives an overview of the religion, history, culture and situation of the Muslim peoples of the Philippines in the late 1970s. It runs to nearly 300 pages and was published by New Day in 1979.

Gowing explains the terms "Muslim Filipinos" and "Moros" as names for all Filipinos who are Muslims, as distinct from Christian Filipinos. A Mindanao annotated bibliography describes the book as a way to correct the lack of information, misunderstandings and wrong ideas about the Moros that were common among other Filipinos.

books.title: Understanding Islam and Muslims in the Philippines
books.summary: Essays on Islam as it is lived in the Philippines, collected and edited by Peter Gowing.
books.overview:
This collection of essays on Islam and Muslims in the Philippines was edited by Peter G. Gowing and published by New Day Publishers in Quezon City in 1988.

It is in 3 parts. The first, on Islam, covers Islam in a society of many religions, relations between church and mosque, the history of Islam in Southeast Asia, and the early contacts of Mindanao and Sulu with the outside world. The second, on Muslim Filipino ethnology, has an essay on the anthropology of Christianity and Islam in the Philippines. The third, on Muslims and the Philippine nation, takes in the Moro wars, the conflict in Cotabato, Maguindanaon views at the constitutional convention, the Philippine state and Muslim ideas, development in Mindanao and Sulu, and the prospects for peace in the Muslim South.

The book was reviewed in the Journal of Asian Studies in 1989 and the Journal of Southeast Asian Studies in 1991.

books.title: The Sulu Zone, 1768–1898
books.subtitle: The Dynamics of External Trade, Slavery, and Ethnicity in the Transformation of a Southeast Asian Maritime State
books.summary: The Sulu Sultanate at its height as a trading state: the China trade in sea produce, the slave raiding that fed it, and the peoples it drew in, from Spanish, British and Dutch archives. The book that made the Sulu Zone a field of study. Second edition 2007.
books.overview:
James Francis Warren's book studies the "border zone" around the Sulu and Celebes Seas from 1768 to 1898, and its ties with China and the West. He shows how the China trade changed the Sulu Sultanate. It brought organised, long-distance slave raiding at sea, and captives were absorbed into a Malay Muslim society on a scale not seen before.

Warren rebuilds the social, economic and political ties among the many peoples of the zone, with the sultanate at its centre. He questions labels such as "piracy", "slavery", "ethnicity" and "the state". The publisher notes that he gives a place to people historians often leave out: forest dwellers, highlanders and slaves, and the fishers, raiders, divers and traders of everyday life.

Warren is a professor of history and Southeast Asian studies at Murdoch University in Australia. The book first appeared in 1981. NUS Press brought out a second edition of 440 pages in 2007.

books.title: Iranun and Balangingi
books.subtitle: Globalization, Maritime Raiding and the Birth of Ethnicity
books.summary: The Iranun and Balangingi raiders of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, the world economy that called their raiding into being, and how a way of life became an ethnic name.
books.overview:
This history looks at the Sulu and Mindanao region, the "Sulu Zone", from the late 18th century. It shows how world trade, long-distance sea commerce, raiding and the flight of refugees shaped its peoples. It follows Iranun raiding from its beginnings to the organised slaving of the 19th century, and the rise of the Balangingi and other seafaring groups.

James Francis Warren, a historian of Southeast Asia at Murdoch University, wrote it as a companion to his earlier book The Sulu Zone (1981). He draws on archives and published works, and on period testimony, diaries, interviews and his own fieldwork in the Philippines, Indonesia and Malaysia.

The book offers a way to understand how ethnic identity forms, and why it matters for political conflict in the region today. It was nominated for a national book award in the Philippines.

books.title: Triumph of Moro Diplomacy
books.subtitle: The Maguindanao Sultanate in the 17th Century
books.summary: Sultan Kudarat’s Maguindanao as the Dutch and Spanish records show it: a sultanate that held its own between two empires by diplomacy as much as by war.
books.overview:
Ruurdje Laarhoven's study looks closely at relations between the Dutch at Ternate and the Maguindanao sultanate in the 17th century. Library records list Dutch activity in Mindanao among its subjects. The book has 267 pages of text plus appendices, notes, a glossary and a bibliography.

A Mindanao annotated bibliography sees its main theme as the politics of a small power against big ones. It shows how the sultanate used practical, shrewd diplomacy to fend off Dutch and other colonial threats to its sovereignty and territory. The same source calls the book a contribution to the scarce writing on Mindanao's local history.

The book was reviewed in the Journal of Southeast Asian Studies, and by Leonard Andaya in Asian Perspectives in 1992.

books.title: Magindanao, 1860–1888
books.subtitle: The Career of Datu Uto of Buayan
books.summary: Datu Uto, who ruled the upper Pulangi against the Spaniards in the last decades of their rule, and what his rise and fall show of Maguindanao politics. Ileto’s first book, reissued by Anvil in 2007.
books.overview:
This is Reynaldo Ileto's study of Datu Uto, the ruler of Buayan on the upper Pulangi in the late 19th century. It grew out of his master's thesis at Cornell University in 1970 and was first issued in 1971 as a Data Paper of Cornell's Southeast Asia Program. Mindanao State University's University Research Center reprinted it in 1984 with a new foreword.

The book is at once a local history, an account of relations between Spain and Magindanao, and a biography of a Magindanao orang besar, or great man. Ileto rebuilds Uto's career by reading the contradictions in the Spanish colonial sources. He shows a leader who was more than the Spaniards' picture of a petty tyrant. At the height of his power the Spaniards dealt with Uto as an equal, and a treaty with Spain recognised his authority over Buayan and Buluan.

Ileto, who studied at the Ateneo de Manila and Cornell, later became known for Pasyon and Revolution.

books.title: The Institutions of Maguindanao
books.summary: The sultanate, the datus, the law and the ranks of Maguindanao society, set out from Spanish sources and the author’s ethnographic fieldwork.
books.overview:
Ghislaine Loyré wrote this short study of the political institutions of the Maguindanao sultanate. The Historical Conservation Society in Manila published it in 1991, as number 53 in its series. It forms Part 6, Volume 1 of the society's General History of the Philippines and runs to 83 pages.

Loyré, who also wrote as Ghislaine Loyré-de Hauteclocque, studied the Muslims of Mindanao over many years. Her other work includes A la recherche de l'Islam philippin, a book in French reviewed in Philippine Studies in 1994, and articles in that journal on the Spanish fort of Iligan from 1750 to 1760 (1987) and on foreign influences on Muslim rituals (1998).

books.title: Making Mindanao
books.subtitle: Cotabato and Davao in the Formation of the Philippine Nation-State
books.summary: How Cotabato and Davao were drawn into the Philippine state in the first half of the twentieth century, through the datus and settler elites who learned to work it, and what that made of Mindanao politics.
books.overview:
This study compares the provinces of Cotabato and Davao to show how the Philippine state took hold in Mindanao. It covers the American colonial period from 1900 to 1941 and the years after independence up to martial law in 1972.

Patricio N. Abinales argues that local power was shaped by the building of the state, not only by ethnicity or ideology. The state could rule this frontier because the strongmen who controlled it came to terms with each other and with Manila. Southern Mindanao stayed stable until Ferdinand Marcos changed the rules in the late 1960s and early 1970s. The book is a revised version of his doctoral thesis at Cornell University.

Abinales grew up in Ozamiz City and teaches at the University of Hawaii at Manoa. Ateneo de Manila University Press later issued an expanded 20th anniversary edition.

books.title: Orthodoxy and History in the Muslim-Mindanao Narrative
books.summary: Essays questioning the received story of the Moro struggle, the unbroken resistance from Spain to the present, and asking what the record shows instead.
books.overview:
This collection of essays by the political scientist Patricio N. Abinales was published in the Ateneo de Manila University Press's Mindanao Studies series. It runs to about 265 pages.

The essays dispute a common view in both scholarship and activism: that the history of Mindanao is mainly a story of unbroken Muslim resistance to the Philippine state. In its place Abinales offers a set of revisionist arguments. He stresses the lasting ties between Muslims and other Filipinos, the unusual way the state and the economy developed in Muslim Mindanao, the dilemmas facing Muslim separatism, and what can be learned by comparing Mindanao's provinces with each other.

books.title: Mindanao Ethnohistory beyond Nations
books.subtitle: Maguindanao, Sangir, and Bagobo Societies in East Maritime Southeast Asia
books.summary: Maguindanao, Sangir and Bagobo as peoples of one sea rather than of two countries, in a history that crosses the border with Indonesia the way they did.
books.overview:
Shinzo Hayase follows 3 peoples of the seas between Mindanao and eastern Indonesia: the Maguindanao, the Sangir and the Bagobo. The publisher describes the book as tracing how maritime societies that thrived in Southeast Asia's "Age of Commerce" lost their autonomy as modern states took shape, and became minorities within them.

The book first came out in Japanese from Iwanami Shoten in Tokyo in 2003. Ateneo de Manila University Press published this English edition in 2007. It was reviewed in the anthropology journal Anthropos in 2008.

books.title: The Great Island
books.subtitle: Studies in the Exploration and Evangelization of Mindanao
books.summary: Essays on the exploration of Mindanao and the Christian missions there from the sixteenth century on, by a Jesuit historian who spent his later life in Cagayan de Oro.
books.overview:
Miguel A. Bernad's book gathers 9 studies of the exploration and evangelisation of Mindanao. Its full subtitle in library records is "Studies in the Exploration and Evangelization of Mindanao".

The studies run in rough time order. They re-examine the evidence on whether the first mass was held at Butuan or Limasawa, then cover the first church in Mindanao in 1596 to 1597, Father Ducós and the Muslim wars of 1752 to 1759, and the Tamontaca mission in southern Mindanao from 1861 to 1899. Others follow the evangelisation of the Davao region, José Rizal's exile in Dapitan, the exploration of the Rio Grande de Mindanao from 1888 to 1890, and climbs of Mount Apo from 1852 to 1958.

Ateneo de Manila University Press published it in 2004, with references and an index.

books.title: Battle of Marawi, 1895
books.summary: The Spanish assault on the Maranao kotas at Marawi in 1895, from Spanish accounts and Maranao memory, by the Maranao sociologist who founded the university’s research centre.
books.overview:
This short book from Mindanao State University's University Research Center gives an account of the Spanish attack on Marawi in 1895. It also looks back at earlier defences, including the defence of Marawi in 1891, and the stands of Lapulapu at Mactan and Rajah Soliman at Manila.

The author, the Maranao scholar Mamitua Saber, combines Maranao oral tradition with historical documents. A library record notes that he also uses fiction based on facts. An earlier 1980 edition was titled Battle of Marawi, 1895 and Two Related Articles. This enlarged edition adds other historical notes.

books.title: Aristocrats of the Malay Race
books.subtitle: A History of the Bangsa Moro in the Philippines
books.summary: A history of the Moro peoples written from within, from the sultanates to the MNLF, by a Maranao lawyer; printed by the author and much cited in the region. Revised 2001.
books.overview:
Nasser A. Marohomsalic records the Bangsa Moro struggle for self-determination over some 440 pages. He traces it first against Spain, then against the United States, and then against the government of the Filipino majority. He gives that government the Maranao name "beberno a saroang-a-tao", the "government of foreigners".

The book does more than tell a history. It ends with a political proposal: a separate state and government for the Bangsa Moro within a federal system. The author first published it himself in 1995 and issued it again in 2001.

Marohomsalic was a Maranao lawyer. He served as a commissioner of the Commission on Human Rights and was the first Maranao elected National Secretary of the Integrated Bar of the Philippines. At his death he was serving on the National Amnesty Commission.

books.title: The Minoritization of the Indigenous Communities of Mindanao and the Sulu Archipelago
books.summary: How the Moro and Lumad peoples became minorities in their own homeland: the land laws, the resettlement programmes and the migration from Luzon and the Visayas, with the figures.
books.overview:
B. R. (Rudy) Rodil, a Mindanao historian, asks how the Moro and Lumad peoples, once the majority in Mindanao and Sulu, came to be minorities in their own homeland. He looks at colonial and Philippine land laws, government resettlement programmes and the large migration of settlers from Luzon and the Visayas, and gives the population figures.

The Alternate Forum for Research in Mindanao in Davao City first published the book in 1994, at 123 pages. A revised and longer edition of 174 pages followed in 2004. Both have a bibliography, and library records file the book under ethnic relations, government policy and the legal status of minorities.

books.title: A Story of Mindanao and Sulu in Question and Answer
books.summary: Mindanao’s history for the general reader, in questions and short answers: who was here first, how the settlers came, where the conflict began.
books.overview:
Historian B. R. (Rudy) Rodil tells the history of Mindanao and Sulu as a series of questions and answers. The Mindanao Coalition of Development NGO Networks (MinCODE) in Davao published it in 2003. The book runs to 277 pages and includes a bibliography of more than 10 pages. Mindanao State University's history course on the region's Muslims and indigenous peoples lists it as a reading.

Rodil, known as Ompong, was the son of Tagalog migrants and grew up in Upi, Maguindanao, among the Teduray and the Moro. He taught at Notre Dame of Sulu and Ateneo de Davao, then spent 23 years in the history department of MSU-Iligan Institute of Technology until he retired in 2007. He sat on the 1988 Regional Consultative Commission that helped draft the organic act for the autonomous region, and twice served on the government panel in talks with the Moro National Liberation Front between 1993 and 1996.

His writing aimed to bring Moro and Lumad history into the mainstream, to correct labels of them as pirates and savages, and to build relations among Mindanao's 3 peoples.

books.title: Kalinaw Mindanaw
books.subtitle: The Story of the GRP-MNLF Peace Process, 1975–1996
books.summary: The twenty-one years of talks between the government and the Moro National Liberation Front, from Jeddah to the 1996 Final Peace Agreement, by a historian who sat on the government panel.
books.overview:
This book tells the story of the peace talks between the Philippine government and the Moro National Liberation Front from 1975 to 1996, ending with the Final Peace Agreement. "Kalinaw" means peace. The Alternate Forum for Research in Mindanao published it in Davao City in 2000, with maps and illustrations.

The author, B. R. (Rudy) Rodil, is a Mindanao historian and peace advocate who took part in the government's negotiations with the MNLF and later the MILF. He wrote it to show that the path of peace is not only desirable but doable, and costs far less in lives and money than war. In 2020 MindaNews ran a revised version of the book in 18 parts in his column.

books.title: The Lumad and Moro of Mindanao
books.summary: A short report for an international readership on the two peoples displaced by the settlement of Mindanao and the state of their claims in the early 1990s.
books.overview:
This 1993 report for the London-based Minority Rights Group looks at the 2 groups of peoples native to Mindanao, the Lumad and the Moro, and their struggle over land and self-rule. It is a short report of about 35 pages, with maps.

After a glossary and a brief political history of the Philippines, it introduces the Lumad and Moro and their origins. It then covers land ownership and settlement programmes, the effects of big business and development, and the Moro journey towards self-determination. 2 case studies look at the Lumad fight over Mount Apo and the cost of the Agus I hydroelectric plant. The report closes with prospects for peace and directions for the future.

Rudy Rodil taught history at MSU-Iligan Institute of Technology and had taught in Jolo. He was born in Maguindanao and grew up among the Tiruray, a Lumad people. Ed Garcia of the University of the Philippines helped complete the report.

books.title: Revolt in Mindanao
books.subtitle: The Rise of Islam in Philippine Politics
books.summary: A journalist’s account of the Moro revolt of the 1970s, the MNLF and the Marcos government’s war, written as it happened.
books.overview:
T. J. S. George, a journalist who was then editor of Asiaweek in Hong Kong, wrote this history of the Muslim separatist movement in the southern Philippines. Oxford University Press published it in Kuala Lumpur in 1980, while the war between the Marcos government and the Moro National Liberation Front was still going on.

The publisher presented it as the first attempt at a full history of the subject written for general readers rather than scholars. The book compares Spain and the United States as colonial rulers. It finds early Philippine leaders lacking in understanding of Islam and accuses Mindanao's traditional Muslim leaders of seeking their own advantage. It looks at episodes such as a politician's plan for a new sultanate in Sabah, a Christian army officer who posed as a Muslim in Sulu, and the secret army that ended in the Jabidah massacre. It also examines the part played by Arab countries.

George argues that the split between Muslims and Christians, and the divisions among Muslims, could be resolved, and that a settlement favouring Mindanao's Muslims was within reach.

books.title: Muslim Separatism
books.subtitle: The Moros of Southern Philippines and the Malays of Southern Thailand
books.edition: Ateneo de Manila University Press edition, 1990
books.summary: The Moro and Patani Malay movements side by side: their histories, their organisations and what each state did about them, in the first full comparison of the two.
books.overview:
W. K. Che Man compares 2 separatist movements: the Moros of the southern Philippines and the Malays of southern Thailand. He treats each as a political movement that grew out of ethnic minorities' discontent with the state.

The book looks at how each resistance took shape and developed, and at its structure, leaders and ideas. It gives special weight to the role of Islam in starting and sustaining both. Che Man questions the view, held by both modernisation theorists and Marxists, that ethnic identity will fade over time. He argues that a state's push for one "national culture" can leave minority groups outside it.

Oxford University Press published the book in 1990.
books.blurb: This important comparative study views the separatist movements in the Philippines and Thailand as both political phenomena and springing from dissatisfied ethnic minorities. The author questions "Modernization school" and Marxist belief that ethnicity is a transitory phenomenon, arguing that that concept of "national culture" may result in minority groups remaining outside the culture. Examining the form and development of these resistance struggles, this study investigates their structure, leadership, and ideology, and highlights the role of Islam in shaping and sustaining the movements.

books.title: Swish of the Kris
books.subtitle: The Story of the Moros
books.edition: Reprinted by Orchid Press, 2009, and Cerberus Books, 2011
books.summary: A popular history of the Moros and their wars with Spain and the United States, by an American who had lived in Zamboanga; vivid, partisan and long the only book of its kind in English.
books.overview:
This is a popular history of the Moros and their long wars, written for American readers by Vic Hurley and published in New York by E. P. Dutton. Library records list its subjects as the Muslims of the Philippines and the history of Mindanao.

Hurley went to the Philippines in 1925 and started a coconut plantation in the interior of Mindanao, which failed. He then spent 7 years in Zamboanga managing American companies and was made an honorary third lieutenant in the Philippine Constabulary. He left in 1934 and drew on these years for this book and for Jungle Patrol, his history of the Constabulary.

The book has been reprinted, including by Orchid Press in 2009 with photographs and maps from the author's own collection, and by Cerberus Books.

books.title: Myself and a Few Moros
books.summary: The memoir of a US Army officer posted to Sulu at the start of American rule, and what he made of the datus and the people he was sent to govern. Out of copyright and free to read.
books.overview:
Sydney A. Cloman was a US Army officer who, in 1899, landed at Bongao in Tawi-Tawi with 3 officers, a contract surgeon and 185 men of the 23rd Infantry. American forces were then busy fighting in Luzon, and Cloman's small garrison was sent to take over from the departing Spanish in the far south of the Sulu archipelago. This memoir tells of his time there.

The book is made up of 10 light, anecdotal chapters, among them "Bongao", "A Trip Among My Islands", "My First Bribe, and Others", "Selungun", "Moro Romances" and "Visits to Royalty". They describe his dealings with local datus, traders and the Sultan of Sulu. Photographs show Jolo, Siasi, Sitangkai and Samal villages, Sultan Jamalul Kiram II and Hadji Butu.

Cloman says in his foreword that he wrote it for 2 young relatives and favoured a good story over strict accuracy. His colonial-era views of the Moro people show throughout, so it reads best as a record of how an American officer saw Sulu, not as a history of it.

books.title: Moroland, 1899–1906
books.subtitle: America’s First Attempt to Transform an Islamic Society
books.summary: The first years of the American occupation of the Moro country, from Bates’s treaty with the Sultan of Sulu to Bud Dajo, told campaign by campaign from the army’s records.
books.overview:
Robert Fulton tells how the US Army came to govern the Moro lands after the Spanish-American War. At first the Americans worked through the traditional rulers and respected Islamic law. Later the aim shifted to remaking Moro society in an American image. Moro Province became a military-governed Islamic colony inside the largely Christian Philippine Islands. The Moros resisted what they saw as an attack on Islam and their way of life, and more than a decade of battles and expeditions followed.

Fulton built the book on research in the original army files. It covers the rivalry between Leonard Wood and John J. Pershing and the 1906 massacre at Bud Dajo on Jolo. Fulton concludes that the United States failed to pacify and transform the Moros largely because Wood abandoned a policy of accommodation with Moro leaders that Fulton links to Pershing.

A review by Robert Mihara of West Point questioned how the book uses its sources. A 2009 revised edition added 6 chapters and carried the story to 1920.

books.title: The Moro War
books.subtitle: How America Battled a Muslim Insurgency in the Philippine Jungle, 1902–1913
books.summary: The American campaigns against the Moros under Wood, Bliss and Pershing, from Bud Dajo to Bud Bagsak, as a military history for the general reader.
books.overview:
James R. Arnold tells the story of the American war against the Moros of Mindanao and Sulu from 1902 to 1913. The library record describes it as covering the fierce debates between military men and peace advocates, the problems US forces faced, and the role of the future general John Pershing.

The book has 20 chapters in time order. It begins with "A place called Moroland", first contacts and the Battle of Bayan. It then follows the rise of Pershing, the governorship of Leonard Wood and the killing at Bud Dajo, the quieter years under Tasker Bliss, jungle patrols, and Pershing's return. It ends with Bud Bagsak, "the last battle".

The closing chapters, "A forgotten war" and "The cradle of leadership", look at what the campaign meant for the American officers who served in it. The book has notes, a bibliography and an index.
books.blurb: Documents the early twentieth-century battle against Muslim insurgents in the southern Philippines, discussing the fierce debates between military supporters and peace advocates while offering insight into the challenges faced by U.S. forces and the contributions of future general John Pershing.

books.title: Making Moros
books.subtitle: Imperial Historicism and American Military Rule in the Philippines’ Muslim South
books.summary: How the American officers who ruled the Moro Province wrote its people into a story of savagery and progress, and used that story to govern.
books.overview:
This book looks at how American officers made Muslim colonial subjects of the Moros during the military rule of the southern Philippines, from 1899 to 1913. Michael C. Hawkins argues that ideas of time, history and evolution, more than simple ideas of race, guided how Americans studied, sorted and tried to remake the Moros. He also shows Moros taking part in shaping their own identity as modern subjects.

The 4 chapters cover American "imperial taxonomies", the disruption of Moro society and the campaign against slavery and debt bondage, capitalism offered as a cure, and modernity and colonial guilt. An epilogue looks at how this period is remembered.

Hawkins draws on archives in the United States and the Philippines. A review in the Journal of Southeast Asian Studies noted how the book shows ordinary Moros living through American policy.
books.blurb: "This book offers a unique look at the colonial creation of Muslim subjects during the early years of American rule in the southern Philippines. It examines the Islamic Philippines during its most formative period in modernity--a period indispensible to discussions of integration in the Filipino Islamic South"--

books.title: American Datu
books.subtitle: John J. Pershing and Counterinsurgency Warfare in the Muslim Philippines, 1899–1913
books.summary: Pershing’s years among the Maranao and in Sulu, as a captain at Lake Lanao and as governor of the Moro Province, and the mix of diplomacy and force he learned there.
books.overview:
This book follows John J. Pershing's years in the southern Philippines between 1899 and 1913, through his military campaigns among the Moros. Ronald K. Edgerton shows how American ideas of counterinsurgency changed in the first long military encounter between the United States and Muslim fighters.

Pershing put less weight on so-called civilising efforts. He built relationships with local Moro leaders and took part in Moro customs, and Moros made him a datu. Edgerton argues that he came to see that no single method fits every place, and that tactics must suit local conditions. The press notes that the book gives voice to Filipino Muslims in their dealings with American officers, and sets Pershing's approach against harsher calls for force. The author also calls for a rethink of more invasive methods used by US officers against Muslim militants today.

Edgerton is professor emeritus of history at the University of Northern Colorado. He lived in the Philippines as a Peace Corps volunteer and a Fulbright scholar, and wrote People of the Middle Ground, a history of central Mindanao.

books.title: Civilizational Imperatives
books.subtitle: Americans, Moros, and the Colonial World
books.summary: The American project in the Moro South set against the other colonial empires of its day, and the Moros’ own uses of it, from the archives of three continents.
books.overview:
Oliver Charbonneau, a historian of the United States at the University of Glasgow, studies American colonial rule over Mindanao and the Sulu archipelago in the early 20th century. He argues that American power in the Moro South rested on a vision of transforming the people it ruled, with violence at its centre. He links the project to American settler conquest in North America and to the European and Islamic empires of the time.

After an introduction, 7 chapters cover how Americans imagined the Moro and the land, colonial courtrooms, clinics and settlements, schools, "corrective violence" including massacre and punishment, how colonists kept up their own spaces and bodies in the tropics, Moros who visited the United States in fact and fiction, and Mindanao-Sulu's ties to the wider world. A conclusion looks at what colonial rule left behind.

The book appeared in Cornell's series The United States in the World in 2020. Ateneo de Manila University Press published a Philippine edition.

books.title: People of the Middle Ground
books.subtitle: A Century of Conflict and Accommodation in Central Mindanao, 1880s–1980s
books.summary: A hundred years in the Bukidnon–Lanao borderlands, where Maranao, Lumad, settlers and the state met and sometimes made terms.
books.overview:
Ronald K. Edgerton's history covers a century of conflict and accommodation in Central Mindanao, from the 1880s to the 1980s. Library records place its focus on Bukidnon: its history, social life, customs and folklore.

The publisher's description centres on people who learned to borrow from the new without losing touch with the old. It asks how they found a middle ground in a world of fast change. Ateneo de Manila University Press published the book in 2008. Patricia Irene Dacudao reviewed it in the journal Philippine Studies.

books.title: Moro Warrior
books.subtitle: A Philippine Chieftain, an American Schoolmaster, and the Untold Story of the Most Remarkable Resistance Fighters of World War II in the Pacific
books.summary: The Moro guerrillas of Cotabato and Lanao in the Second World War, led by Edward Kuder’s foster son Mohammad Adil and the American schoolteacher himself, pieced together from their papers and the memories of those who fought.
books.overview:
This narrative history tells of the Moro resistance to the Japanese occupation of Mindanao from 1942 to 1945. At its centre are Mohammad Adil, a Moro guerrilla leader, and his foster father Edward Kuder, an American schoolteacher and colonial official who wrote about the Moro fighters after the war.

Thomas M. McKenna is an anthropologist who lived and worked in Moro communities in Mindanao. He met Adil near Cotabato City in 1986 and began his research then. The book rests largely on Adil's memories, checked against written sources, including documents Adil made in his guerrilla camps. McKenna says no events were invented, though he filled in some details.

The story also reaches forward to Adil's part in resisting the Marcos government's offensive in the early 1970s. The book was published in the United States and by Ateneo de Manila University Press in the Philippines.

books.title: The Filipino Muslim Armed Struggle, 1900–1972
books.summary: The Moro revolts from the American conquest to the eve of martial law, by the historian who would lead the National Historical Institute.
books.overview:
Samuel K. Tan's study of Moro armed resistance from the start of American rule in 1900 to 1972, the year martial law was declared, was published by the Filipinas Foundation in 1977. It runs to about 200 pages. Tan had earlier covered the years up to 1941 in The Muslim Armed Struggle in the Philippines, 1900–1941 (1973).

Tan, born in Siasi, Sulu, in 1933 of Chinese, Tausug and Sama parentage, taught history at the University of the Philippines for 3 decades and later chaired the National Historical Commission. He wrote more than 20 books, many of them on the history of the Muslim South.

books.title: Decolonization and Filipino Muslim Identity
books.summary: What decolonisation meant for a people who did not see the republic as their own, and how a Filipino Muslim identity was argued over in the decades after independence.
books.overview: Samuel K. Tan, a historian who chaired the Department of History at the University of the Philippines, looks at what decolonisation meant for Muslims in the Philippines. His subject is how a Filipino Muslim identity was argued over in the decades after independence, by a people many of whom did not see the republic as their own. The book was published in Quezon City in 1989 by the UP Department of History. Tan also wrote A History of the Philippines and other works on Philippine and Muslim history.

books.title: Internationalization of the Bangsamoro Struggle
books.summary: How the Moro cause reached the Organisation of the Islamic Conference and the Muslim world, and what the attention did to the movement at home. Revised 1995.
books.overview:
Historian Samuel K. Tan's study of the Moro secessionist movement looks at how the Bangsamoro struggle reached beyond the Philippines. A library abstract says it covers the movement's historical roots, its emergence as an organised movement in 1968, its different names and divisions, and its strengths and weaknesses.

Tan notes that the secessionist idea counts all the people of Mindanao as part of the Bangsamoro. The UP Center for Integrative and Development Studies and the University of the Philippines Press published the book in 1993. A revised edition followed in 2003.

books.title: Surat Sug
books.subtitle: Letters of the Sultanate of Sulu
books.summary: The Sulu Sultanate’s own correspondence in Jawi, transcribed and translated in two volumes: letters to Spain, Britain and its own datus from the last century of its independence.
books.overview:
This work presents letters of the Sultanate of Sulu in the Tausug language, written in Jawi and in roman script, with English translations and notes in English. The first volume covers the sultanate itself (Kasultanan). The second has sections for the datus (Kadatuan), the hajis (Kahadjian) and others.

The compiler, Samuel K. Tan, was a historian of Chinese, Tausug and Sama parentage, born in Siasi, Sulu, in 1933. He taught history at the University of the Philippines, led its Mindanao Studies Program and chaired the National Historical Institute, which published the work in 2005.

books.title: The Muslim South and Beyond
books.summary: Tan’s later essays on the history and historiography of the Muslim South, collected at the end of his career.
books.overview:
This book collects selected essays by Samuel K. Tan, published by the University of the Philippines Press in 2010. The essays move from general questions about the Mindanao conflict to more specific ones, and keep returning to the central place of the Muslim South in the problem. The book runs to about 185 pages.

Tan was born in Siasi, Sulu, in 1933, of Chinese, Tausug and Sama parentage. He taught history at UP from 1963 to 1994, chaired its history department, directed UP's Mindanao Studies Program and later chaired the National Historical Commission. He wrote more than 20 books. A national historical society credited him with helping readers see the Muslim South as part of the national story.

books.title: The Qur’an and Islamic Manuscripts of Mindanao
books.summary: A study of handwritten Qur’ans, prayer books and kitabs kept by families in Lanao, with what they show of how Islam was learned and copied in the region.
books.overview:
This monograph, number 10 in a series from the Institute of Asian Cultures at Sophia University in Tokyo, studies handwritten Qur'ans and other Islamic manuscripts kept in Mindanao. Midori Kawashima edited it. The contributors are Tirmizy E. Abdullah, Annabel Teh Gallop, Kawashima herself, Ervan Nurtawab and Labi Sarip Riwarung.

The chapters examine particular manuscripts from Lanao. Abdullah writes on the Qur'an of Bayang and the Qur'an of Bacong in Marantao. Riwarung writes on the Qur'an and prayer scroll of Guro sa Masiu. Library records file the book under Arabic manuscripts and Islamic illumination, the decoration of manuscripts, in Mindanao. It ends with a bibliography.

books.title: History of the Moro and Indigenous Peoples in MinSuPala
books.summary: A Moro teacher’s history of the peoples of Mindanao, Sulu and Palawan, written as a textbook and printed by the author.
books.overview:
Ben J. Kadil's history covers the Moro and indigenous peoples of Minsupala, the name for Mindanao, Sulu and Palawan taken together. It appeared in 2002, at 228 pages, with references. Library records name Kadil as publisher, while a course module cites it as issued in Marawi City by the university's Office of the Vice Chancellor for Research and Extension.

It is a reading for History 003, the Mindanao State University course on the Filipino Muslims and indigenous peoples of Minsupala. A module for that course lists it beside Peter Gowing's Muslim Filipinos: Heritage and Horizon, Cesar Adib Majul's Muslims in the Philippines and Rudy Rodil's A Story of Mindanao and Sulu in Question and Answer.

Kadil is a professor in the Department of History and Graduate Studies at Mindanao State University, with a PhD in Philippine Studies from the same university. He later wrote The Moro Wars in the Philippines, 1565 to the Present, on the Mindanao War of 2003 and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front, published by Edwin Mellen Press in 2017.

books.title: Sultanate of Sulu
books.subtitle: The Unconquered Kingdom
books.summary: A Zamboanga writer’s history of the Sulu Sultanate as a state that was never conquered, printed by the author.
books.overview:
This history of the Sulu archipelago, subtitled "a razor-sharp and bold inquiry into the dark side of history", sets out to give readers a working knowledge of the many sides of the Sulu Sultanate. A Mindanao annotated bibliography describes it as a work of historical reflection and a contribution to the small literature on the Moro peoples.

Clemencio Montecillo Bascar is a Zamboanga writer and a former professor and vice president of Western Mindanao State University. He also wrote a companion history of Maguindanao, The Crescent That Spain Failed to Plunder.

books.title: Tausug & the Sulu Sultanate
books.summary: The Tausug and their sultanate seen from Sabah, where many Tausug now live, by a Malaysian writer of Tausug descent; first published in Malay in 2007.
books.overview:
This 222-page history of the Tausug people looks at their part in Islamic civilisation under the Sulu sultanate. It was written by Asreemoro and published by Saba Islamic Media in 2008. Library records list the history and the social life and customs of the Tausug as its subjects, and it includes a bibliography.

The same publisher also issued the book in Malay as Tausug & Kesultanan Sulu. The description of that edition lists the topics it covers: the genealogy of the sultans of Sulu, the true extent of the Sulu kingdom, the struggle for power between the Kiram and Aranan families, the Jabidah killings of 1968, the Moro wars and the claim to Sabah.
books.blurb: History of the Tausug people and their role in Islamic civilization in Sulu Sultanate.

books.title: Under the Crescent Moon
books.subtitle: Rebellion in Mindanao
books.summary: Two journalists’ investigation of the MILF, the MNLF, the Abu Sayyaf and the Mindanao war at the turn of the century, from the camps and the back channels. The book most reporters on the region started with.
books.overview:
Marites Dañguilan Vitug and Glenda Gloria, 2 Filipino journalists, spent time in the conflict areas of Mindanao and Sulu to write this investigation of the Moro rebellion. It was published in 2000 by the Ateneo Center for Social Policy and Public Affairs with the Institute for Popular Democracy, and won a National Book Award in 2001.

The story opens with the 1967 Jabidah massacre, the killing of young Moro recruits trained for a secret plan to take Sabah, which the authors treat as the spark of the rebellion. They follow the foreign states that backed the rebels, including Libya and Malaysia, and the ties of clan, school and politics that ran through the MNLF, the MILF and the Abu Sayyaf. They also document the large sums released to Nur Misuari during his time in government.

A review in the Philippine Star praised the book's investigative reporting but noted that it says little about Mindanao before the conflict. The book has a bibliography and an index.

books.title: Rebels, Warlords, and Ulama
books.subtitle: A Reader on Muslim Separatism and the War in Southern Philippines
books.summary: A reader on the war in the South at the end of the 1990s: the rebel fronts, the clan armies and the religious leaders, with primary documents and the authors’ reporting.
books.overview:
This reader on Muslim separatism and the war in the southern Philippines was published by the Institute for Popular Democracy in Quezon City in 2000. Eric Gutierrez, Kristina Gaerlan and Mara Stankovitch are named as its authors.

It brings together pieces by several writers. Aijaz Ahmad writes on class and colony in Mindanao and on the war against the Muslims. Eric Gutierrez writes on the warlords' battlefields, religion and politics in Muslim Mindanao, the problems of peace, the unfinished jihad and the reimagining of the Bangsamoro. Francisco Gonzales writes on the sultans of a violent land, and Joel Rocamora on dissidence and development. Gutierrez and Marites Dañguilan Vitug look at the ARMM after the peace agreement, and Eliseo Mercado Jr. writes on peace and development.

books.title: The Moro Conflict
books.subtitle: Landlessness and Misdirected State Policies
books.summary: The argument that land, not religion, is at the root of the Moro conflict: how colonial and Philippine land policy dispossessed the Moros and why the peace deals have not touched it. Free to read.
books.overview:
This East-West Center policy study offers a political and economic explanation of the conflict in the southern Philippines. It starts from 2 observations: Muslim areas have high poverty and social exclusion, and "entrepreneurs in violence" there enforce their own rules over property. The authors trace both to the very unequal ownership and control of land, rooted in colonial history.

The chapters cover settlement, migration and displacement, mass poverty, entrepreneurs in violence, and current land policies, followed by lessons. Tables give population trends from 1918 to 1970 and land distribution figures from the agrarian reform and environment departments.

The authors argue that redistributive land reform must be a central part of any lasting peace, joined to Moro and Lumad ancestral domain claims and to support services for poor farmers. They say neither successive governments nor the main Moro fronts have dealt with the land question.
books.blurb: The conflict in the southern Philippines is becoming increasingly complex, and untangling the knots for a greater understanding of the problem is no easy task. Yet underlying all these manifestations of a complex conflict is a straightforward political-economic explanation. This study argues that the continuing war, the persistence of poverty and landlessness, and the emergence of “entrepreneurs in violence” are mere symptoms of something that has not yet been sufficiently addressed by a succession of Philippine governments or even by mainstream Moro revolutionary organizations: the highly skewed distribution of ownership and control over land resources in the southern Philippines.

books.title: Forging Sustainable Peace in Mindanao
books.subtitle: The Role of Civil Society
books.summary: What civil society groups did and could do for peace in Mindanao, by the Asia Foundation’s long-serving Philippines representative. Free to read.
books.overview:
Policy Studies 17 from the East-West Center Washington asks what civil society groups have done, and could do, for peace in Mindanao. It was written for the Center's project on managing internal conflicts in Asia. Steven Rood was then the Asia Foundation's country representative in the Philippines.

Rood takes civil society broadly, from development NGOs to church groups and business associations, and traces peace work back to the Marcos years in the 1970s. After a short account of the conflict, he describes these groups and their networks, then their peace activities: dialogue between Muslims and Christians, local "spaces for peace", and efforts to shape national peace policy. Closing sections weigh their effects and draw lessons, with a background note on the Moro conflict.

He finds their impact so far indirect and limited. Muslim civil society is weaker than its Christian counterpart, most groups work within one community, and Christian peace groups do not reflect wider Christian opinion. He still argues that civil society matters, and recommends strengthening it, especially on the Muslim side.

books.title: The Moro Reader
books.subtitle: History and Contemporary Struggles of the Bangsamoro People
books.summary: Essays by Moro and Filipino scholars on the Bangsamoro’s history, the right to self-determination and the peace talks, from the Center for People Empowerment in Governance.
books.overview:
This reader was edited by Bobby M. Tuazon for the Center for People Empowerment in Governance (CenPEG), a policy centre based at the University of the Philippines Diliman. In his introduction Tuazon says the idea came in 2007, after CenPEG monitored the elections in the ARMM, at a time when the government-MILF talks had stalled over ancestral domain. The aim was to revive public awareness of the Bangsamoro struggle and give a reference for people's organisations, human rights groups, academics and the media.

Its 12 chapters include essays on colonialism and resistance, "multiple colonialism" in Moroland, the choice between independence and autonomy, ancestral domain as the core issue, neoliberal globalisation, and the Bangsamoro right to self-determination by Abhoud Syed Lingga. There is an annotated conversation with Nur Misuari, and chapters on Moro political dynasties, Muslim women in Palawan, and songs of resistance. Other writers include Julkipli Wadi, Temario Rivera and Kenneth Bauzon.

Long appendices reprint key documents, from the Qudarat-Lopez treaty to the Tripoli Agreement, the 1996 final agreement with the MNLF, and the 2008 memorandum on ancestral domain.

books.title: Bangsamoro sa Malapitan
books.summary: The Bangsamoro struggle explained in Filipino for a national readership, from the sultanates to the MILF talks.
books.overview:
Bangsamoro sa Malapitan: Pagpupunyagi sa Sariling-Pagpapasya is Lualhati M. Abreu's account, in Filipino, of the Bangsamoro struggle for self-determination. It was edited by Bonifacio P. Ilagan and published in 2011 by the Center for People Empowerment in Governance (CenPEG), with a note by MILF peace panel chair Mohagher Iqbal.

In a review for CenPEG, E. San Juan Jr. describes the book's path. It opens with a survey of Moro ethnolinguistic groups and the Lumad, with special attention to the Iranun and Maguindanao. It then turns to the ARMM and the creation of Shariff Kabunsuan province. From there it takes up ancestral domain, which San Juan sees as the central question of the whole book and of the talks with the MILF. Abreu also criticises land reform in the ARMM, and a chapter faces the prejudice of the Filipino majority against the Moro.

San Juan notes that Abreu respects Islamic law and adat while writing from a secular, historical point of view. The book has maps and a bibliography.

books.title: Bangsamoro: A Nation under Endless Tyranny
books.summary: The Moro Islamic Liberation Front’s own history of the Bangsamoro, from the sultanates through colonial rule to the MNLF and the MILF, written by its chief negotiator under a pen name. The third edition of 1999 is the one usually cited.
books.overview:
This is a history of the Bangsamoro written from inside the Moro struggle. Its 12 chapters run from the early peoples and the birth of the sultanates, through Spanish invasion, American rule and annexation to the Philippines, to settlement, displacement and war in Mindanao and Sulu. The last chapters follow the peace talks with the MNLF and the MILF. Appendices include population tables and a list of massacres by the Ilaga.

Salah Jubair joined the Moro movement in 1972 as a young graduate and rose in the MNLF. He later sat on the MILF Central Committee and chaired its information committee. He began the book when the MILF was based in Pakistan. The first edition appeared in Lahore in 1984, a revised one in 1997 and the third, published in Kuala Lumpur, in 1999.

In his foreword Michael O. Mastura gives the book's core thesis: that "the Moros are a wronged people".

books.title: The Long Road to Peace
books.subtitle: Inside the GRP-MILF Peace Process
books.summary: The talks between the government and the MILF from 1997 to the eve of the Memorandum of Agreement on Ancestral Domain, from inside the Front’s panel.
books.overview:
This 250-page book by Salah Jubair, the pen name of Mohagher Iqbal, covers the formal peace talks between the government and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front. It was published in 2007 by the Institute of Bangsamoro Studies.

Jubair writes from inside the MILF, and Iqbal later chaired the Front's negotiating panel. He covers what happened at the negotiating table and also efforts outside the formal talks to find a lasting end to the conflict in Mindanao. A Mindanao annotated bibliography recommends it to readers who want to understand the talks between the government and the MILF.

books.title: Bangsamoro Quest
books.subtitle: The Birth of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front
books.summary: The government–MILF talks from February 1997 to June 2010, told by a Maguindanaon historian and lawyer who sat on the Front’s peace panel.
books.overview:
Datu Michael Mastura, a Maguindanaon historian and lawyer, was a senior member of the MILF peace panel when he wrote this book. In his prologue he calls it an inside account of the talks between the government and the MILF, from 23 February 1997 to 3 June 2010. In May 2012 he gave copies to members of the government panel across the table.

It was published in 2012 by the Southeast Asia Conflict Studies Network and Research and Education for Peace at Universiti Sains Malaysia in Penang. A review in the Asia Mindanaw journal of Ateneo de Zamboanga described it as a mix of reconstructed historical narrative and political analysis of nationalist and separatist movements, with legal and policy proposals, written from Mastura's own point of view.

books.title: Muslim Filipino Experience
books.subtitle: A Collection of Essays
books.summary: Early essays by Mastura on Moro history, law and politics, from the years before he entered Congress.
books.overview:
Muslim Filipino Experience is a collection of essays published in Manila by the Ministry of Muslim Affairs in 1984, as number 3 in its Philippine Islam series. It runs to about 285 pages.

Michael O. Mastura is a lawyer and writer from Cotabato and a descendant of Sultan Kudarat. In 1981 he became the first Deputy Minister of the Ministry of Muslim Affairs. He was a delegate to the 1971 Constitutional Convention and later represented the First District of Maguindanao and Cotabato City in Congress from 1987 to 1995.

books.title: The Rulers of Magindanao in Modern History, 1515–1903
books.subtitle: Continuity and Change in a Traditional Realm in the Southern Philippines
books.summary: The Magindanao Sultanate across 388 years, rebuilt from its own law code and genealogies by a lawyer and historian descended from Sultan Kudarat.
books.overview:
Datu Michael Ong Mastura reconstructs the dynastic history of the Magindanao Sultanate from 1515 to 1903. The book opens with a question: how likely was it that the ancient Filipinos developed a concept of statehood at precolonial contact? To answer it, Mastura draws on the luwaran, the sultanate's code of law, and the tarsila, its genealogies, and combines ethnography with politics.

The press describes the book as a longue durée in the manner of Braudel, looking at the ecology, economy, politics and culture around each ruler. It traces the breaks in the sultanate's politics and the resilience of its traditional authority. It shows the sultanates as regimes that carried the war into Spanish colonial territory, and follows their trade and alliances with the neighbouring mandalas of Southeast Asia.

Patricio N. Abinales, author of Making Mindanao, wrote the foreword and calls it "an exceptional, much-awaited work". The Ateneo de Manila University Press published it in 2023, with a cover by Cielo Castro.
books.note: Also sold as an e-book, ISBN 9786214482450.

books.title: The Moro Armed Struggle in the Philippines
books.subtitle: The Nonviolent Autonomy Alternative
books.summary: A Maranao political scientist’s case, made in the early 1990s, that autonomy won by politics could answer what the armed struggle had not.
books.overview:
This study by Macapado A. Muslim, who later became president of Mindanao State University, looks at the causes of the Moro armed struggle. It argues for peaceful processes that would lead to "autonomy with compensatory justice" for the Moros within the Philippine community.

The book places responsibility on both the armed government and the armed rebels to build a nonviolent institution that answers the needs of all. It proposes a forum to help resolve the conflict without violence and to bring about structural change. It was published by the Office of the President and the College of Public Affairs of Mindanao State University, and was reprinted in 2017.

books.title: The 2018 Bangsamoro Organic Law in the Philippines
books.summary: A reading of the Bangsamoro Organic Law and the government it creates, by a former president of Mindanao State University.
books.overview:
Macapado Abaton Muslim, a former president of the Mindanao State University system and long-time chancellor of MSU General Santos, wrote this book to help end the Bangsamoro armed struggle. He also wanted to share the Philippine experience of managing ethnic conflict with other diverse countries. Its subtitle sums up his case: solving the Mindanao conflict with autonomy plus compensatory justice. Retired Chief Justice Reynato Puno wrote the foreword.

The 120-page book has 6 chapters. After an introduction, it looks at ways of managing cultural diversity, such as assimilation and multiculturalism, and compares regional autonomy and federalism in other countries. It then traces the peace process from the Marcos years to the present and sets out the key features of the Bangsamoro Organic Law, from its Shari'ah courts and fiscal autonomy to transitional justice.

The author argues that territorial autonomy can resolve ethnic conflict when it combines self-rule, power sharing and compensatory justice. For the law to succeed, he calls for ethical leadership, large capacity-building and livelihood programmes for MILF and MNLF members, independent monitoring, and wider support among Christian Filipinos.

books.title: The Moro Islamic Challenge
books.subtitle: Constitutional Rethinking for the Mindanao Peace Process
books.summary: Whether the Philippine Constitution can accommodate the Moro demand for self-rule, and what would have to change, by a human rights lawyer who worked the peace process for years.
books.overview:
Soliman M. Santos Jr., a human rights lawyer long involved in the Mindanao peace process, asks whether the Philippine Constitution can make room for the Moro demand for self-rule. The book revises his 2000 master of laws thesis at the University of Melbourne.

It moves in 6 steps: the constitutional obstacles to a settlement with Islamic rebels; the Moro problem, with the tri-people make-up of Mindanao and the failures of past talks; the Islamic Conference's mediation; sources of hope in the Constitution and in Islamic concepts; a framework of accommodation, with a Bangsamoro Islamic region and a treaty device; and constitutional talks as intercultural dialogue.

The University of the Philippines Press published it in 2001, with a glossary, appendices, a bibliography and an index. In his Philippine Daily Inquirer column, Randy David wrote that Santos reads the Constitution and Islamic law side by side to find shared values, and surveys international law on minority and indigenous rights, self-determination and autonomy. Tim Lindsey of the University of Melbourne noted how it joins constitutional theorists such as Tribe and Tully with scholars of Islam.

books.title: Dynamics and Directions of the GRP-MILF Peace Negotiations
books.summary: The government–MILF talks as they stood in 2005: the agreements so far, the sticking points and the roads open.
books.overview:
Soliman M. Santos Jr. gives a detailed view of the formal peace talks between the Government of the Republic of the Philippines and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front, as they stood in 2005.

A library description says the book reviews relations between the government and the MILF through clear stages and phases. It also gives key facts and analysis of the negotiations and of how agreements were carried out on the ground. The Alternate Forum for Research in Mindanao in Davao City published it in 2005, with a bibliography of more than 10 pages.

books.title: The Road to Peace and Reconciliation
books.subtitle: Muslim Perspective on the Mindanao Conflict
books.summary: Moro voices on the conflict and what peace would take, gathered for the Asian Institute of Management by a Tausug former cabinet member.
books.overview:
This book gathers research papers and speeches by Muslim political and religious leaders, scholars and former rebels. They came out of a year-long study and a series of conferences and workshops at the Asian Institute of Management. It was edited by Amina Rasul, then a research fellow of the AIM Policy Center and a former presidential adviser on youth affairs. Former president Fidel Ramos wrote the foreword.

The papers look at instability and poverty in Mindanao, and at how to balance secular and religious political demands. The book also sets out the participants' recommendations, to help policy makers and programme staff find ways to end the conflict.

One main recommendation is a referendum among Muslims to choose between independence, greater autonomy or federalism. In her preface Rasul writes that "Muslims must be allowed to live according to their beliefs and principles".

books.title: Broken Peace?
books.subtitle: Assessing the 1996 GRP-MNLF Final Peace Agreement
books.summary: Ten years after the agreement with the MNLF, what was delivered and what was not, in studies commissioned by the Philippine Council for Islam and Democracy.
books.overview:
10 years after the 1996 Final Peace Agreement between the government and the Moro National Liberation Front, Amina Rasul asks why it had not brought the peace it promised. The government said it had met its obligations, while the MNLF spoke of broken promises. This study aims at a fact-based assessment that goes beyond blame. The 314-page book was published in 2007 with the Philippine Council for Islam and Democracy, the Konrad Adenauer Stiftung and the Magbassa Kita Foundation.

The study opens with why peace agreements so often fail, then tells the story of the 1996 agreement and earlier attempts such as the 1976 Tripoli Agreement. It examines the legal and political structures set up and how the agreement was carried out, including fiscal support from the national government. It compares the government and MNLF views, reviews foreign aid to the ARMM, and assesses human development a decade on.

Presenting the research in 2007, Rasul argued that unemployment had worsened and that ARMM development indicators were as bad as before the agreement. She also argued that the region had less autonomy than its people had hoped for.

books.title: Costly Wars, Elusive Peace
books.subtitle: Collected Articles on the Peace Processes in the Philippines, 1990–2007
books.summary: Essays written across two decades of the Philippine peace processes, with the Moro fronts and with the communists, by the scholar who would chair the panel that signed the Comprehensive Agreement.
books.overview:
Miriam Coronel-Ferrer, a political science professor at the University of the Philippines Diliman, collects her articles on the Philippine peace processes from 1990 to 2007. The publisher describes them as covering the first 2 decades of armed conflict and peacebuilding after Marcos. They assess the major armed conflicts and the talks with the Moro fronts and the communist rebels under successive presidents. They also cover the part played by civil society, the integration of former combatants into society, and the unfinished business of regional autonomy in Mindanao.

The book came out from the University of the Philippines Press in 2013. By then the author had joined the government panel negotiating with the MILF in 2010 and had become its chief negotiator in December 2012.

books.title: Region, Nation and Homeland
books.subtitle: Valorization and Adaptation in the Moro and Cordillera Resistance Discourses
books.summary: How the Moro and Cordillera movements each made a homeland out of a region, and adapted their claims to the state they fought, compared.
books.overview:
Miriam Coronel-Ferrer looks at the Moro and Cordillera movements in the Philippines as they told their own story. The publisher notes that such movements tell stories of oppression and liberation, criticise those in power and offer their own vision of the homeland they hope to build. In both regions, the identities the movements built and their claims to self-determination differed from group to group and changed over time.

For the Moro side, she traces how the language of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front borrowed from and answered that of the Moro National Liberation Front, from which it broke away. For the Cordillera, she follows the turn to stronger ethnic nationalism in the Cordillera People's Liberation Army after it split from the Cordillera People's Democratic Front. She ends by asking where these movements stand now and which of their ideas still matter.

Coronel-Ferrer is a professor of political science at the University of the Philippines. As chair of the government peace panel, she signed the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro in 2014. ISEAS published the book in 2020.

books.title: Rido
books.subtitle: Clan Feuding and Conflict Management in Mindanao
books.summary: The first systematic study of rido, the clan feuds that take more lives in Muslim Mindanao than the rebellion, with case studies from Lanao, Maguindanao, Sulu and Basilan and the ways communities settle them. Expanded edition from Ateneo de Manila University Press in 2014; the original is free to read.
books.overview:
This volume gathers studies of rido, the feuds between families and clans in Mindanao, marked by repeated acts of revenge. The research was done by Mindanao civil society groups and universities with support from USAID and The Asia Foundation, and edited by Wilfredo Magno Torres III.

The first 3 chapters inventory rido cases in 11 provinces, including Maguindanao and Lanao del Sur. Together they record 1,266 cases that killed over 5,500 people and displaced thousands. Other chapters look at how the Tausug, Maguindanao, Maranao, Sama and Yakan manage clan conflict, with case studies from Baloi, Lanao del Norte, and from Maguindanao and North Cotabato. The causes they find include elections, land disputes, crimes against chastity and simple jests.

The 2014 expanded edition adds essays, among them a comparison of Tausug and Corsican feuding, and an epilogue by Torres on rido management.

books.title: Insurgents, Clans, and States
books.subtitle: Political Legitimacy and Resurgent Conflict in Muslim Mindanao, Philippines
books.summary: Why the conflict keeps returning: the clans, the rebel fronts and the state as rival sources of authority in Muslim Mindanao, and the shadow economy that sustains all three.
books.overview:
Francisco J. Lara Jr. asks why Moro rebels who gained political power could not keep their authority and legitimacy. Lara was Philippine country director of International Alert, the UK-based peacebuilding group. The 340-page study was published in the Ateneo de Manila University Press's Mindanao Studies series.

Lara shows how rebels who gave up their arms in exchange for formal office could not compete with powerful clans and local elites. Those clans offered basic security and took a growing share of internal revenue allotments under devolution. They also allowed a shadow economy to spread, which strengthened their power and let people earn a living with little state taxation.

The book draws 2 unsettling conclusions. Political legitimacy may come less from building a strong state than from weakening it, and less from building peace than from showing an ability to use violence. The publisher presents it as useful to anyone studying insurgency, local state-building and political settlements elsewhere.

books.title: Out of the Shadows
books.subtitle: Violent Conflict and the Real Economy of Mindanao
books.summary: The shadow economies of Mindanao, from guns and drugs to the informal credit and trade that ordinary people live by, and how they feed and are fed by the conflict. Free to read.
books.overview:
This book from International Alert reports research on the links between violent conflict and the informal, or "shadow", economy of Mindanao. It was edited by Francisco Lara Jr. and Steven Schoofs and supported by the Australian aid agency AusAID. It was launched in Manila in January 2013.

Its case studies cover the trade in illicit firearms, kidnapping for ransom, informal land markets, illicit cross-border trade, the traditional credit system and illicit drug markets. The book asks why these shadow economies are so resilient, and how they affect the chances for peacebuilding, development and democratic change.

The authors note that shadow economies are a large part of Mindanao's economy but had been largely left out of analyses of its conflict. They argue that the region's political and economic problems cannot be understood or solved without bringing the informal economy into the picture.

books.title: Breaking the Links between Economics and Conflict in Mindanao
books.summary: A discussion paper on the economic roots of the Mindanao conflict and what business and donors could do about them. Free to read.
books.overview:
This discussion paper by Sylvia Concepción, Larry Digal, Rufa Guiam, Romulo de la Rosa and Mara Stankovitch was presented at the Waging Peace conference in Manila in December 2003. It came from International Alert's Business and Conflict Programme.

It has 4 chapters. The first traces the roots of the conflict, including dispossession, poverty, discrimination and political exclusion, and the peace efforts from the Tripoli Agreement to the Arroyo government. The second looks at Mindanao's economy, the gaps between regions and the economy of Muslim areas. The third sets out what war costs: displacement, lost services, and the trade in arms, illegal logging and kidnapping for ransom.

The last chapter asks what business can do to break these links. It uses case studies such as Datu Paglas and the ARMM and Mindanao business councils, and ends with recommendations to business and government.

books.title: Primed and Purposeful
books.subtitle: Armed Groups and Human Security Efforts in the Philippines
books.summary: Profiles of 14 armed groups in the Philippines, the communist and Moro fronts, the Abu Sayyaf and the clan militias among them, with what is known of their arms and their effect on the people around them. Free to read.
books.overview:
This book looks at the armed groups behind the Philippines' 2 main internal conflicts: the nationwide communist insurgency and the Moro insurgency in Muslim Mindanao. It was written by Soliman M. Santos Jr. and Paz Verdades M. Santos with other contributors, and edited by Diana Rodriguez. The South-South Network for Non-State Armed Group Engagement and the Small Arms Survey published it together.

Part 1 has thematic chapters on peace talks, ceasefires, counter-terrorism, the Abu Sayyaf, disarmament and reintegration, state and private armed groups, and small arms control. Part 2 profiles 14 rebel groups, among them the MNLF, the MILF, the Rajah Solaiman Movement and the Abu Sayyaf.

The book also explains how guns reach these groups: leaks from government stocks, open borders, local gunsmiths and weak rules. It argues that armed groups are part of the human security problem but must also be part of the solution.
books.note: Edited by Diana Rodriguez.

books.title: Mindanao
books.subtitle: The Long Journey to Peace and Prosperity
books.summary: Scholars on the peace process as it stood after the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro: the deal, the economy, the clans, the law, and what would be needed to make the Bangsamoro work.
books.overview:
This volume, edited by Paul D. Hutchcroft of the Australian National University, looks at the peace process between the government and the Moro fronts under President Benigno Aquino III. Agreements signed in 2012 and 2014 raised hopes of peace, but the process stalled after the botched Mamasapano operation in early 2015. The book examines that stage of the process and the history, politics and economics behind the conflict.

After Hutchcroft's introduction, the chapters are by people involved in the process and those who study it. Ronald Holmes assesses the Aquino years, and Patricio Abinales critiques the received view of war and peace. Steven Rood looks at international actors, and Miriam Coronel Ferrer writes on the compromises behind the peace settlement. Abhoud Syed Lingga writes on building the Bangsamoro government, and Edilberto and Melinda de Jesus on "the Mamasapano detour". Toby Monsod looks at human development in the ARMM, and Francisco Lara at the shadow economy and strongman rule.

It was published by Anvil in Manila in 2016 and later by World Scientific.

books.title: Voices from Moro Land
books.subtitle: Perspectives from Stakeholders and Observers on the Conflict in the Southern Philippines
books.summary: Essays by people inside the conflict and those who study it, Moro scholars, MILF writers and foreign observers among them, gathered by two German researchers.
books.overview:
Peter Kreuzer and Rainer Werning, 2 German researchers, edited this collection of essays by people involved in or close to the conflict in the southern Philippines. It was published in Malaysia in 2007 by the Strategic Information and Research Development Centre.

The editors open with an overview of the "zig-zag path from war to peace". Werning then looks at how the German media covered the 2000 kidnappings from Sipadan. Julkipli Wadi writes on Southeast Asian regional security and the Mindanao conflict. Abhoud Syed M. Lingga contributes 2 essays, on Bangsamoro self-determination and on the role of third parties in the peace process. Salah Jubair writes on the MILF's peace talks with the government, and Philipp Bück on civil society and the conflict. Ishak Mastura writes on peace and development in the ARMM and on security, ethnic conflict and the United States in the South. Michael Mastura closes with an essay on political Islam in the 21st-century Philippines.

books.title: Political Clans and Violence in the Southern Philippines
books.summary: How the clans of Muslim Mindanao hold power through violence, and why the state lets them, in a report from the Peace Research Institute Frankfurt. Free to read.
books.overview:
This is PRIF Report No. 71, written in 2005 by Peter Kreuzer of the Peace Research Institute Frankfurt. Its main argument, as library abstracts describe it, is that the war in the south cannot be understood from political and economic causes alone. Local dynamics also matter.

Kreuzer treats violence between clans and political families as a layer of conflict of its own, alongside the struggle for independence, and older than the rebellion. He shows how clans can use the armed groups of the civil war to pass off their own political feuds as acts of war. The report runs to about 40 pages.

books.title: Conflict in Moro Land
books.subtitle: Prospects for Peace?
books.summary: Essays from a Penang conference on the Mindanao conflict after the collapse of the 2008 ancestral domain agreement.
books.overview:
