This collection of essays, edited by Arndt Graf, Peter Kreuzer and Rainer Werning, looks at the Moro conflict and the chances for peace.

Rainer Werning opens with the long history of the conflict. Epifanio San Juan Jr. writes on Moro identity and self-determination, and Peter Kreuzer on how the civil war links to local violence. Other chapters ask whether Muslim members of Congress serve their voters or act as local power brokers, and look at the MILF's strategy between jihadism and negotiation. There are also chapters on how the Indonesian Muslim press and the foreign media covered the conflict and the Abu Sayyaf, and on the future of the ARMM.

books.title: The Mindanao Conflict
books.summary: Papers from the Southeast Asian Conflict Studies Network on the roots of the conflict and the peace process to 2005.
books.overview:
This 203-page collection, edited by Kamarulzaman Askandar and Ayesah Abubakar, was published in 2005 by the Southeast Asian Conflict Studies Network. It brings together papers by scholars and practitioners on the conflict in Mindanao and the efforts to end it.

Miriam Coronel Ferrer opens with the Philippine state and Moro resistance, and Abhoud Syed M. Lingga follows with the Mindanao peace process. Soliman M. Santos Jr. writes on Malaysia's role in the talks between the government and the MILF, and Ayesah Abubakar on keeping the peace. Later chapters cover the Bangsamoro ancestral domain (Lualhati Abreu), peace zones in Mindanao (Zosimo Lee), identity and conflict among the Lumad (Albert Alejo) and the Ligawasan marsh (Tarhata Mapandi).

books.title: Peace for Mindanao
books.summary: A second collection from the Penang peace programme, on the talks, the ceasefire and civil society’s part in them.
books.overview: This collection was edited by Kamarulzaman Askandar and Ayesah Abubakar and published in 2009 by Research and Education for Peace at Universiti Sains Malaysia in Penang with the Southeast Asian Conflict Studies Network. It came out of a seminar called Consolidation for Peace (COP3) for Mindanao: Strategic Planning for Peace Post MOA-AD. That is, it was planned after the government-MILF memorandum on ancestral domain collapsed in 2008. The papers deal with the peace talks, the ceasefire and the role of civil society, and include references.

books.title: Strategies and Tactics of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front
books.summary: How the MILF fought and negotiated, read as strategy, from a doctoral thesis by a scholar who now heads research at the Development Academy of the Bangsamoro.
books.overview:
Shamsuddin L. Taya studies the political, military and economic strategies and tactics of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front in its fight to free the Bangsamoro homeland from the Government of the Republic of the Philippines. The book grew out of his 2006 PhD thesis at the International Islamic University Malaysia, which covered the years 1994 to 2005 and used an organisational approach.

It has 6 chapters: the historical background of the conflict; the MILF's structure, goals, capabilities and constraints; its political strategies; its military strategies and tactics; its economic strategies; and a conclusion. Taya drew on newspapers, speeches, press releases, joint communiqués, peace agreements and interviews with informed people.

He finds the MILF's strategies effective. They kept a splinter group alive and made it the strongest liberation movement in the region, a force that the government and regional and international players must reckon with. Penerbit Universiti Utara Malaysia published the book in 2009. Taya was a visiting scholar at that university from 2007 to 2019 and later headed the research division of the Development Academy of the Bangsamoro.
books.blurb: This book reveals the strategies and tactics of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) in the Southern Phillipines. It looks at the political, military and economic strategies and tactics of the MILF in its quest to liberate the Bangsamoro homeland and its people from the clutches of the Government of the Republic of the Phillipines (GRP) and its agents.

books.title: The Sulu Arms Market
books.subtitle: National Responses to a Regional Problem
books.summary: The trade in guns across the Sulu and Celebes seas, who sells, who buys and what the Philippines, Malaysia and Indonesia have done about it.
books.overview:
This book studies the illegal gun trade of the Sulu Arms Market, in the border seas between the Philippines, Malaysia and Indonesia. The market has run for centuries. It both sends guns out, to conflicts and crime across Asia and the Pacific, and takes them in, to Mindanao, the Maluku Islands and parts of Malaysia.

Its 6 chapters explain the illegal arms market as a system, name the players and look at supply and demand. The players include criminal gangs, communists, Moro independence groups and Islamic militants. The book then reviews what the Philippines, Malaysia and their neighbours have done to stop the trade.

Lino Miani shows that the market is tied to piracy, terrorism and other illegal trade, and that it is a security problem for at least 5 ASEAN countries.

books.title: Between Integration and Secession
books.subtitle: The Muslim Communities of the Southern Philippines, Southern Thailand, and Western Burma/Myanmar
books.summary: The Moros set beside the Malays of Patani and the Rohingya of Arakan: three Muslim minorities on the edges of Buddhist and Christian states, and the roads each took.
books.overview:
Moshe Yegar, a research fellow at the Truman Institute of the Hebrew University, compares 3 Muslim minorities that rose against the states they lived in: the Moros of the southern Philippines, the Patani Malays of southern Thailand and the Rohingya of Arakan in Burma/Myanmar. The book runs to over 460 pages, with maps.

Yegar traces how the Islamic revival after the Second World War and the nationalist movements of Southeast Asia pushed each group towards separatism. He asks whether each wanted communal separation, autonomy or full independence, and what means it had to pursue those goals. The book has a part on each community. The Arakan part covers the Muslims of that region, the Patani part covers the annexation of Patani and the figure of Hajji Sulong, and the Moro part covers the MNLF and the dispute over the Tripoli Agreement. A final chapter looks at autonomy.

books.title: Nur Misuari
books.subtitle: An Authorized Biography
books.summary: The life of the founder of the Moro National Liberation Front, from Jolo and the University of the Philippines to Tripoli, Jeddah and the ARMM governorship, written with his cooperation.
books.overview:
Tom Stern, a medical doctor and visiting fellow at Stanford University's Hoover Institution, wrote this biography of the founding chairman of the Moro National Liberation Front. It draws on his private conversations with Misuari.

The first chapter opens with Misuari receiving the UNESCO Peace Prize and then with his detention in Manila on rebellion charges. The story then turns back to his childhood on an island in the Sulu archipelago, his scholarship to study political science at the University of the Philippines, his master's degree in Asian Studies in 1964, and his years as an instructor there until 1968. Later chapters cover the Jabidah massacre, martial law, the MNLF's struggle under 5 presidents from Marcos to Arroyo, his relations with the Organization of the Islamic Conference, and his term as ARMM governor.

A review by Maria Luisa Saministrado in Xavier University's Kinaadman journal found the book rich in historical detail. She suggested it would be more balanced with interviews of people who disagreed with Misuari.

books.title: Beyond the Cult of Dissidence in Southern Philippines and Wartorn Zones in the Global Village
books.summary: A Filipino anthropologist’s essays against the romance of rebellion, on the South and on war zones elsewhere.
books.overview:
Arnold Molina Azurin follows the peace talks of the mid-1990s between the Ramos government and the Moro National Liberation Front under Nur Misuari. The book's prologue opens with a series of bombings around Zamboanga City and asks what they were meant to achieve. Later chapters take up the proposed Southern Philippines Council for Peace and Development, which provinces it should cover, how long it should last, and the objections raised by politicians from Mindanao.

The book has 25 chapters, with titles such as "A Battle of Nerves", "Into the Fray", "Turnaround Time" and "A Nonfinal Chapter", followed by an epilogue, a long appendix, notes on sources and an index. It also reaches back to earlier movements such as the Muslim Independence Movement founded by Udtog Matalam.

The UP Center for Integrative and Development Studies and the University of the Philippines Press published it in 1996. It runs to 360 pages. Library records file it under the MNLF, Muslim political activity and autonomy movements in Mindanao.

books.title: Understanding Mindanao Conflict
books.summary: A veteran Cotabato journalist’s columns on the conflict and the peace talks, collected: forty years of watching from close up.
books.overview:
This book gives a journalist's reading of the Mindanao conflict. Much of it is made up of commentaries Patricio P. Diaz wrote for MindaNews, including on the peace negotiations from 2000 to 2003. A Kasarinlan review describes it as his critical account as a journalist and as a settler who had lived in Mindanao since the last years of American rule. Diaz himself says it is not a scholarly work.

Diaz worked for decades in Cotabato journalism. He was a columnist and later editor of the Mindanao Cross from 1952 to 1989, edited Mindanao Kris and wrote the "Comment" column for MindaNews from its start in 2001. MindaNews presents the book as an attempt to explain the roots and many sides of the conflict.

books.title: State of Local Democracy in the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao
books.summary: An assessment of how democracy works, and does not, in the ARMM’s provinces and towns, by the University of the Philippines’ public administration college with International IDEA and the Philippine Council for Islam and Democracy.
books.overview:
This 260-page report is a citizen-led assessment of how democracy works in the ARMM. It uses the State of Local Democracy framework of International IDEA. The UP National College of Public Administration and Governance and the Philippine Center for Islam and Democracy (PCID) led the work, with Australian aid. It was the 5th in a series of Philippine democracy assessments and the first to look at local democracy. Edna E. A. Co led a team that included Amina Rasul, Mehol Sadain, Rufa Guiam and Benedicto Bacani.

The findings rest on focus group discussions, round tables, surveys, interviews, document review and validation workshops. After a long chapter setting the region in context, the report assesses representative democracy and then participatory democracy. It ends with a summary and recommendations drawn from participants.

Participants valued their freedoms, including freedom of faith in a mostly Christian country, but saw democracy in the ARMM as even more flawed than in the rest of the Philippines. The report points to deep poverty and to leaders who used autonomy to keep their hold on power and wealth instead of serving their people.

cover.source: Philippine Center for Islam and Democracy

books.title: Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro
books.summary: The peace agreement signed in Malacañang on 27 March 2014 between the Government of the Philippines and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front, with its annexes on transition, revenue, power sharing and normalisation. Free to read.
books.overview:
The Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro is the final peace agreement between the Government of the Philippines and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front. It was signed at Malacañang Palace on 27 March 2014, after 17 years of talks, 12 of them facilitated by Malaysia. It brings together the agreements the 2 sides signed along the way: the Framework Agreement on the Bangsamoro of October 2012, its 4 annexes on Transitional Arrangements and Modalities, Revenue Generation and Wealth Sharing, Power Sharing and Normalization, and the Addendum on Bangsamoro Waters.

The agreement runs on 2 tracks. On the political track, a new autonomous Bangsamoro would replace the ARMM. Of 81 listed powers, 58 would go to the Bangsamoro, 9 would stay with the central government and 14 would be shared. On the normalization track, the MILF would decommission its armed wing, the Bangsamoro Islamic Armed Forces. The agreement led, through the Bangsamoro Organic Law, to the creation of the BARMM in 2019.

books.title: Republic Act No. 11054
books.subtitle: The Bangsamoro Organic Law
books.summary: The law, signed on 26 July 2018 and ratified in January 2019, that created the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region and its parliamentary government. Free to read at the Lawphil Project.
books.overview:
Republic Act No. 11054 is the Organic Law for the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao. It repealed the earlier organic acts of the ARMM, Republic Act No. 6734 and Republic Act No. 9054. Its preamble speaks of the aspirations of the Bangsamoro people and other inhabitants of the region to an enduring peace built on justice, within the Constitution and the sovereignty of the Republic.

The law has 18 articles. They cover Bangsamoro identity, the region's territory, the powers of the regional and national governments and how they relate, the Bangsamoro government and its Wali, basic rights, the justice system including Shari'ah courts, security and public order, fiscal autonomy, the regional economy, rehabilitation and development, the plebiscite, and the Bangsamoro Transition Authority.

Some key provisions: a Parliament of 80 members, half of them representatives of political parties elected by proportional representation; an annual block grant equal to 5% of net national internal revenue and customs collections; and a Transition Authority of 80 members appointed by the President and led by the MILF, to govern during the transition.

books.title: Marawi Siege
books.subtitle: Stories from the Front Lines
books.summary: The five-month battle for Marawi in 2017, from the soldiers, hostages, residents, officials and former fighters who lived it, by a defence journalist who covered it day by day.
books.overview:
This book reports the 5-month battle for Marawi in 2017. Carmela Fonbuena, a journalist who covered defence and was at the front lines, describes the fighting in a crowded city where snipers and landmines were everywhere.

She tells the story through many eyes: soldiers, hostages, displaced civilians, local officials, the MILF and former Maute Group fighters. The first chapter, "The Raid", was published by the Philippine Center for Investigative Journalism.

The book was one of 5 nominees for the 2021 Witold Pilecki International Book Award.

books.title: The Battle of Marawi
books.summary: The siege of Marawi as the people who fought it and lived through it remember it, by a journalist who has followed the military in Mindanao for thirty years.
books.overview:
Journalist Criselda Yabes tells the story of the battle for Marawi, fought from 23 May to 23 October 2017 between the Armed Forces of the Philippines and fighters aligned with ISIS. The book opens with the military raid to capture Isnilon Hapilon that set off the wider battle. It draws on hundreds of interviews Yabes did after the fighting with soldiers, aviators, marines and others affected by it. She wrote it with a research grant from the Harry Frank Guggenheim Foundation.

Most chapters are stand-alone accounts of close-quarters fighting, mixed with sections on senior officers making plans and decisions, and some on Hapilon and the Maute group. Maps and diagrams show the chain of command and troop movements through the city. Battalion and company commanders appear only under nicknames; only generals are named.

It was Yabes's 10th book and the first title of Pawikan Press, a Davao City imprint for books on Mindanao and Palawan. A second edition followed in 2021. A Canadian Army Journal reviewer found it a good grounding for general readers, though historians would need other sources for finer detail.

books.title: The Marawi Siege and Its Aftermath
books.subtitle: The Continuing Terrorist Threat
books.summary: The Islamic State-aligned groups that took Marawi, what became of them afterwards, and the threat they still pose, by a Philippine security analyst.
books.overview:
Rommel Banlaoi, a Philippine security analyst who teaches international studies at Miriam College, edited this short volume on the 2017 siege of Marawi. It has 5 chapters by 3 writers on terrorism and security.

Kumar Ramakrishna traces how the "East Asia Wilayah" of ISIS came to Marawi. Banlaoi follows the Abu Sayyaf Group from its birth to its ties with al-Qaeda, ISIS and Jemaah Islamiyah, and its mix of terrorism and crime. Amparo Pamela Fabe writes 2 chapters: one on how the siege was financed, and one on a trauma counselling project for Maranao women and children displaced by the fighting.

In the closing chapter Banlaoi argues that terrorism in Mindanao is far from resolved despite the military victory. He calls for better use of anti-terrorism programmes, more public awareness and community-based approaches to the causes of extremism. A review in the Kyoto Review of Southeast Asia found the book timely but said some chapters needed deeper research.

books.title: Marawi, the “East Asia Wilayah” and Indonesia
books.summary: A report, written while the siege was on, on who the Marawi fighters were, how Indonesians and Malaysians joined them, and what it meant for the region. Free to read.
books.overview:
This is IPAC Report No. 38, dated 21 July 2017, 2 months into the battle for Marawi. It traces how pro-ISIS groups grew in the Philippines, moved their base to Lanao del Sur and took over the city, with sections on their use of social media, their funding and their ties to ISIS in Syria.

The report finds that the Marawi operation got money directly from ISIS central. It describes a chain of command that ran from Syria, through Katibah Nusantara, the Southeast Asian unit led by the Indonesian Bahrumsyah, to a Malaysian, Dr Mahmud Ahmad, who handled recruits and funds in Marawi. Several sections follow Indonesian networks, including fighters who trained on Basilan, and police arrests in Indonesia.

It warns of a higher risk of attacks in Philippine cities, Indonesia and Malaysia, and of new leaders emerging from returning fighters. An appendix gives a partial list of Indonesian fighters in Mindanao.

books.title: Marawi and Other Poems
books.summary: Poems by a Cebuano poet and retired judge, the title poem among them written on the siege of Marawi.
books.overview:
This is the 10th poetry collection of Simeon Dumdum Jr., a poet and former trial court judge in Cebu City. It was published by Bughaw, an imprint of Ateneo de Manila University Press.

The title poem, written in long lines set in groups of 3, describes the attackers who came "pounding their way through Marawi, waving black flags" and seized a priest. The rest of the book ranges widely: home life, travel, nature and figures from popular culture. The poems use many forms, among them the haiku, sonnet, villanelle, sestina, ballad and the Korean sijo.

books.title: How the Spaniards Won in Marawi but Lost in Cavite
books.summary: The Spanish campaigns against the Maranao in the 1890s, set against the revolution that broke out in Luzon at the same time.
books.overview:
Rey Luis Adeva Montesclaros gives an account of 2 major Spanish military campaigns in Lanao: the Weyler campaign of 1891 and the Blanco campaign of 1895. He says the recent destruction of Marawi moved him to write it, as proof that history keeps repeating itself in Lanao.

His main argument links Lanao to Luzon. Spain sent 5 of its 7 army regiments in Mindanao against the Maranao, and this left its forces near Manila weak when the 1896 Revolution broke out. Cavite fell as a result. In his view, Spain might have beaten the Katipunan had its troops not been tied down in the south.

The 222-page book also fills a gap in the history of northern Mindanao. It covers the work of the Spanish religious orders there and the hardships of migrant settlers, who faced Maranao resistance because they were seen as tools of Spanish rule. The author offers these lessons to policymakers and others dealing with Mindanao today.

books.title: In the Presence of My Enemies
books.summary: A year as a hostage of the Abu Sayyaf in the jungles of Basilan, by the American missionary whose husband was killed in the rescue that freed her.
books.overview:
Gracia Burnham and her husband Martin, a missionary pilot, worked in the Philippines with New Tribes Mission. In this memoir, written with Dean Merrill, she tells of the year and 11 days they were held hostage by the Abu Sayyaf in the Philippine jungle, together with other captives. The book also covers their courtship, marriage and mission work before the kidnapping.

It ends with a failed rescue attempt in which army fire killed Martin and Ediborah Yap, a nurse who was the other remaining hostage. Gracia was shot in the leg and survived. Publishers Weekly called the memoir honest and unaffected. It said she describes the captors' beheadings of hostages and forced "marriages" without dramatising them, writes frankly about her own faith at its highs and lows, and shows respect for people of other faiths. She wrote the book in part to keep her husband's legacy of faith alive. A later paperback edition adds a chapter on what came after.

books.title: Peace Warriors
books.subtitle: On the Trail with Filipino Soldiers
books.summary: Years on the road with the army in Mindanao and Sulu, and the soldiers who found themselves building schools as often as fighting.
books.overview:
Peace Warriors: On the Trail with Filipino Soldiers is journalist Criselda Yabes' account of time spent in the field with Philippine Army officers and soldiers in Mindanao. She earlier wrote The Boys from the Barracks, about the military after EDSA.

A review by a young army officer describes it as true stories of officers, soldiers and other key figures in Mindanao, both Muslim and Christian, set against the MILF, the MNLF and the Abu Sayyaf. It shows how soldiers lived in the field, and how they fit into the search for lasting peace. "Mindanao is complex," Yabes writes. "Every village, every town, every province has a story of its own." Library records give Anvil Publishing as the publisher, with a date of 2011.

books.title: Below the Crying Mountain
books.summary: A novel of Sulu in the 1970s, of a Tausug family and the war that came to Jolo. It was longlisted for the Man Asian Literary Prize and won the UP Centennial Literary Prize.
books.overview:
This novel is set in Jolo during 2 bloody days in February 1974, under martial law, when the town burned in the fighting. It follows 2 women: Rosy France, a mestiza from Zamboanga who falls in love with a rebel leader called the Professor, and Nahla, a young Tausug woman. The Professor is a fictional figure modelled on Nur Misuari.

Criselda Yabes is a Filipino journalist and author who also wrote The Battle of Marawi. The novel won the University of the Philippines Centennial Literary Prize and was longlisted for the 2010 Man Asian Literary Prize. Penguin later republished it under the title Crying Mountain.

books.title: Muslim Rulers and Rebels
books.subtitle: Everyday Politics and Armed Separatism in the Southern Philippines
books.summary: An anthropologist’s account, from years in Cotabato City, of how ordinary Maguindanaons lived the rebellion, the datus and the state, and why the separatist story and the everyday one do not match. Free to read in the University of California Press e-books collection.
books.overview:
Thomas McKenna asks a question most accounts of the Moro struggle skip: what were ordinary Muslims fighting for? The anthropologist did field research in Cotabato City, mainly in 1985–86, with return visits in 1988 and 1995. He combines this fieldwork with history to look at the gap between Muslim leaders and the people they claimed to lead.

The book has 11 chapters. The early ones trace Islamic rule in Cotabato, Spanish and American colonial rule, and what McKenna calls "the myth of Morohood". The later chapters follow the separatist rebellion, the war as seen from the community of Campo Muslim, the unarmed struggle, and Muslim nationalism after Marcos.

McKenna argues that separatist leaders won popular support in Cotabato because the established datus had done nothing to protect ordinary Muslims from the effects of massive Christian migration. Yet ordinary Muslims often resisted the changes to custom and ritual that movement leaders promoted. Their support for the rebellion did not mean they accepted every idea of those who led it.

books.title: The Tausug
books.subtitle: Violence and Law in a Philippine Moslem Society
books.summary: The classic ethnography of the Tausug of Jolo: feud, friendship, law and honour as they were lived in the 1960s. Kept in print by Waveland Press.
books.overview:
Thomas Kiefer, an American anthropologist, wrote this short ethnography of the Tausug of Jolo for Holt, Rinehart and Winston's Case Studies in Cultural Anthropology series in 1972. Waveland Press later reprinted it.

The book studies a society in which, in its own words, violence was an everyday occurrence. It describes the kinds of violence found among the Tausug, the situations that set it off, and how a man could restore his standing after an insult or injury. It then follows how disputes and feuds spread through the wider community and shaped its social life.

books.title: The Sea People of Sulu
books.subtitle: A Study of Social Change in the Philippines
books.summary: The boat-dwelling Sama Dilaut of Tawi-Tawi in the 1960s and the changes already reaching them, from the anthropologist who lived among them.
books.overview:
H. Arlo Nimmo's short study, subtitled A Study of Social Change in the Philippines, is based on his fieldwork among the Sama-Bajau of Sulu from 1965 to 1967. It appeared in 1972 in the series Studies in Social and Economic Change.

Nimmo compares the boat-dwelling Sama of Tawi-Tawi with the house-dwelling Sama of Sibutu. He finds clear differences in how households are formed, which marriages are preferred, religious practice, and where power lies in kin groups and villages. The anthropologists at the Human Relations Area Files sum up his finding this way: he traces these differences not to more contact with other cultures, but to the way people reshaped old patterns of behaviour to adapt to a changing political world.

The book has illustrations, a bibliography and an index. Nimmo later wrote The Songs of Salanda, stories drawn from the same fieldwork.

books.title: Magosaha
books.subtitle: An Ethnology of the Tawi-Tawi Sama Dilaut
books.summary: Nimmo’s return to the Sama Dilaut three decades on: the full ethnography of a people who had by then mostly come ashore.
books.overview:
Magosaha sums up H. Arlo Nimmo's research among the Sama Dilaut, the boat-dwelling Sama of the Tawi-Tawi islands. Earlier writers, Nimmo among them, called these people "Badjau" or sea gypsies; in this book he uses the name Sama Dilaut. He first did fieldwork with them in the 1960s, and returned in 1977, 1982 and 1997.

The book records Sama Dilaut boats and houseboats, fishing, households and kin, the yearly round, ritual, shamans, the care of the dead and the honouring of ancestors. Its main argument is about change over 4 decades. The trade in sea and forest products, the spread of Islam, armed rebellion and military occupation together cost the Sama Dilaut much of their material culture, above all their boat-houses and old ways of fishing. They kept, the book finds, their own view of the world and their ties to their ancestors.

Kathleen Nadeau, reviewing it in the Journal of Asian Studies, called it the culmination of Nimmo's life's work. Yale's Human Relations Area Files rates it as excellent primary data.

books.title: Zamboanga and Sulu
books.subtitle: An Archaeological Approach to Ethnic Diversity
books.summary: Excavations and surveys in Zamboanga and Sulu read for what they say of how the region’s peoples came to differ.
books.overview:
Alexander Spoehr uses archaeology to give historical depth to the peoples of the southern Zamboanga peninsula and the Sulu archipelago: the Zamboangueños, Subanun, Tausug, Badjau and Samal-speaking groups. He treats them not as isolated tribes but as societies linked by exchange. Land and forest goods from the Zamboangueños and Subanun met the sea products and trade goods of the Tausug and Samal, and control of trade shaped who held power, with the Tausug sultans and datus at the top.

Spoehr surveyed and dug at Fort Pilar, at rock shelters and caves on the east coast of Zamboanga City, at forts around Parang on Jolo, whose plans he reconstructed, and on Sanga-Sanga in Tawi-Tawi, where finds date to between 5995 and 6650 BC. The rest of the book compares pottery, stone tools, shell ornaments, brass and grave markers. His pottery finds question the archaeologist Solheim's threefold division of Philippine pottery.

It was the first Ethnology Monograph of the University of Pittsburgh's Department of Anthropology, published in 1973, with 298 pages. Eric Casiño reviewed it in Philippine Studies in 1977, and Karl Hutterer in the Journal of Asian Studies.

books.title: The Maranao
books.summary: Essays by Maranao scholars on their own people: the sultanates, the torogan, the darangen, marriage, law and the lake.
books.overview: This collection of essays on the Maranao of Lake Lanao was edited by 2 Maranao scholars, Mamitua Saber and Abdullah T. Madale, and published in Manila by Solidaridad Publishing House in 1975. Library records file it under the social life and customs of the Maranao. The essays deal with their sultanates, the torogan or royal house, the Darangen epic, marriage, law and the lake. The book runs to 141 pages and includes references, and later writers on Maranao folklore have cited it.

books.title: The Maranaws
books.subtitle: Dwellers of the Lake
books.summary: A general account of the Maranao for students and the curious: history, social ranks, arts, beliefs and daily life around Lake Lanao.
books.overview:
Abdullah T. Madale's The Maranaws: Dwellers of the Lake is a general book about the Maranao people of Lake Lanao and their way of life. Rex Book Store in Manila published the first edition in 1997. It runs to 310 pages, with illustrations and photographs, and a bibliography.

Madale, born in 1937, had written about the Maranao for more than 20 years before this book. He co-edited The Maranao with Mamitua Saber in 1975 and wrote The Remarkable Maranaws in 1976. The year before this book he published The Maranaw Torogan, on the traditional houses of the Maranao datus.

books.title: The Maranaw Torogan
books.summary: The torogan, the carved house of the Maranao datu, its building, its okir and the rank it proclaimed.
books.overview:
This illustrated book is about the torogan, the traditional house of the Maranao datus, and its place in Maranao life. Library records list its subjects as Maranao social life and customs, Maranao rites and ceremonies, and the conservation and restoration of traditional houses in Lanao del Sur. Rex Book Store in Manila published the first edition in 1996, in 183 pages with some colour plates and a bibliography.

Readers who have reviewed it online say Madale explains why the torogan was central to Maranao life, and that he also discusses the clash between the old order and the electoral system, and how fast change has affected the Maranao.

The author, Abdullah T. Madale, was born in 1937. He had written on his people for decades: he co-edited The Maranao with Mamitua Saber in 1975, wrote The Remarkable Maranaws in 1976, and followed this book with The Maranaws: Dwellers of the Lake in 1997.

books.title: The Meranao
books.subtitle: A Study of Their Practices and Beliefs
books.summary: A Maranao sociologist’s survey of his people’s customs and beliefs, from birth to burial.
books.overview:
Esmail R. Disoma's study describes the practices and beliefs of the Maranao of the Lanao provinces. The Department of Sociology of the College of Social Sciences and Humanities at Mindanao State University published it in 1990, at 199 pages, with a bibliography. Library records list its subjects as Maranao ethnology, social life and customs, and rites and ceremonies. A later edition was printed by Ivory Printing and Publishing House in Iligan City in 1999.

Later scholars of Maranao literature cite the book for points of custom. It sets out the 4 principalities of the traditional homeland, Unayan, Masiu, Bayabao and Baloi, known together as the pat a pengampong ko Ranao. It records the belief that a girl with many suitors gains honour and prestige and is called kiyadayu'oan. And it describes kapaniwaka, the gift of raw food from the young man's parents to the girl's parents, which families of rank treat as a small wedding and as a way to win the girl and her kin.

books.title: Bangsamoro Society and Culture
books.subtitle: A Book of Readings on Peace and Development in Southern Philippines
books.summary: Readings on the Moro peoples’ history, society and culture assembled for the peace studies programme at MSU-Iligan.
books.overview: Jamail A. Kamlian compiled this book of readings on the history, society and culture of the Moro peoples, for teaching about peace and development in the southern Philippines. It was published in Iligan City in 1999 by the Iligan Center for Peace Education and Research and the university's Office of the Vice Chancellor for Research and Extension, with illustrations and a map. Library records list among its subjects the Moro National Liberation Front and the Tausug. Christine Godinez Ortega reviewed it in the journal Langkit in 2006.

books.title: The Yakans of Basilan Island
books.subtitle: Another Unknown and Exotic Tribe of the Philippines
books.summary: One of the few book-length accounts of the Yakan of Basilan: their farming, weaving, rites and faith as they were in the 1970s.
books.overview:
Andrew D. Sherfan's study of the Yakan people of Basilan carries the subtitle Another Unknown and Exotic Tribe of the Philippines. Fotomatic in Cebu City published it in 1976, in 224 illustrated pages with a short bibliography. Its first chapter gives a general background on Basilan Island. It is still cited as a source on Yakan culture, for example on the Yakan use of Jawi script, pottery and drums.

Andrew Dib Sherfan also wrote on the Lebanese-American poet Kahlil Gibran. His books include Kahlil Gibran: The Nature of Love (1971), and he edited A Third Treasury of Kahlil Gibran (1975).

books.title: The Kalibugans
books.subtitle: Moros of Zamboanga Peninsula
books.summary: The Kalibugan, the Muslim Subanen of the Zamboanga peninsula, and how they stand between the Moro and Lumad worlds.
books.overview:
This study is about the Kalibugan, a Moro people of the Zamboanga peninsula. Its full subtitle calls it an inquiry into social fission, hybridity and ethnicity. It looks at the basic forms of Kalibugan religious life and how they shape farming beliefs.

Rolando C. Esteban wrote it to bring the Kalibugan to national notice. The book also argues for oral history as a research method, showing that oral evidence can stand in history and ethnography. The University of Santo Tomas Publishing House published it in 2002, at 231 pages.

Esteban teaches social anthropology at the University of the Philippines Diliman and edits the Philippine Social Sciences Review. His interests include pioneer settlements in Mindanao, sea migration and everyday ethnicity. In the same year as the book he studied tradition and modernity in a Subanen village, and he later studied social fission, diaspora and ethnicity among a Southeast Asian Muslim minority with a grant from the Toyota Foundation, presenting the findings in Sabah and Sarawak in 2005.

books.title: Tunggal Hulaĥ-Duwa Saraĥ
books.subtitle: Adat and Sharee’ah Laws in the Life of the Tausug
books.summary: How Tausug custom and Islamic law live together in one society, by a Tausug scholar of the University of the Philippines.
books.overview:
Mashur Bin-Ghalib Jundam's book looks at how adat, or customary law, and Islamic law shape Tausug life, in the family and in the community. Vibal Publishing House published it in 2006 and launched it in January 2007 at UP Diliman. Vibal presented it as a detailed guide to Islamic laws and tenets that could also help teach non-Muslims about Islam, at a time when DepEd was bringing Islamic values and madrasah education into the school curriculum. The book runs to 228 pages, with a bibliography and an index.

Jundam is a Tausug from Sulu. He studied at Notre Dame of Jolo College and earned his master's in Asian Studies and his doctorate at the University of the Philippines. He advised the Southern Philippines Council for Peace and Development on education in the ARMM and was dean of the UP Institute of Islamic Studies when the book appeared. It was his first book.

books.title: Mindanao Statecraft and Ecology
books.subtitle: Moros, Lumads, and Settlers across the Lowland-Highland Continuum
books.summary: Mindanao’s three peoples and their politics as shaped by the land they hold, lowland, upland and coast, by a Filipino anthropologist.
books.overview:
Eric S. Casiño is a Filipino anthropologist who did long fieldwork among the Jama Mapun of Cagayan de Tawi-Tawi and other peoples of the southern Philippines. In this book he looks at Mindanao's 3 peoples, the Moros, the Lumads and the settlers, and at how their politics and statecraft relate to the land they hold, from the coast and lowlands to the highlands.

Notre Dame University in Cotabato City published it in 2000, with photographs, a bibliography and an index. Library records file it under the politics and government of the Cotabato region, Muslims in that region, and autonomy and independence movements in Mindanao.

books.title: The Food & Culture of the Tausug
books.summary: Tausug cooking and what it says of Tausug life: the dishes, the occasions and the manners of the table, with recipes.
books.overview: Norma Abubakar Abdulla's book looks at Tausug food and what it shows about Tausug social life and customs in Sulu. The Research and Development Center of Centro Escolar University in Manila published it in 1989. It runs to 215 pages, with illustrations, maps and 6 pages of references. Library records file it under the Tausug people's food, their social life and customs, and the ethnology of Sulu.

books.title: Tausug Cookbook
books.summary: Tausug dishes from a home cook, printed on demand: tiyula itum, pastil, satti and the rest.
books.overview:
This cookbook, subtitled The Best of Home-Cooked Halal Tausug-Filipino Dishes, collects recipes from the author's family, passed down from one generation to the next. Abdulaziz H. Hamsain calls sharing them a lifetime project. His aim, he says, is not only to adapt the family recipes but to preserve and promote the dishes as a part of Tausug culture.

Hamsain is a Tausug who was born and raised in Saudi Arabia and has lived and worked in the Philippines, in the outsourcing industry in Manila. He shows Tausug cooking in videos on YouTube and promotes Tausug culture, history and origins through his website. The book is printed on demand through Blurb. Its international edition, first published on 15 February 2020, has 78 pages in a 6 by 9 inch format, in softcover and hardcover.

books.title: Experiences and Views of Divorced Muslim Women in Jolo, Sulu
books.summary: Interviews with divorced Tausug women on marriage, separation and what the law and the community allowed them.
books.overview: Jennifer Saipudin Nandu's short study looks at the experiences and views of divorced Muslim women in Jolo, Sulu. It is a revised version of her 2001 master's thesis at De La Salle University. It was published in 2003 in the university's Health Social Science book series, with support from the Ford Foundation, and runs to 82 pages.

books.title: Trafficking in Women and Children in Zamboanga, Basilan, Sulu, and Tawi-Tawi
books.summary: A study of trafficking across the Zamboanga–Sulu corridor to Sabah and beyond, its routes and its victims, by the Ateneo Human Rights Center.
books.overview:
The Ateneo Human Rights Center carried out this study with support from the United Nations Global Initiative to Fight Human Trafficking. Its foreword notes that the port of Zamboanga City had become a major hub for people trafficked to Malaysia and beyond, yet had been little studied. The writers were Amparita Sta. Maria, Nina Patricia Sison-Arroyo and Rhealeth Krizelle Ramos.

The team interviewed 31 people: 22 actual or potential victims and 9 officials and service providers. It also held round table discussions in Zamboanga City and Bongao, wrote case studies and analysed documents. The results describe the victims, the push and pull factors, the traffickers and the trafficking experience. A further chapter looks at how government agencies enforce and prosecute under the anti-trafficking law, and at weak points in Philippine agencies, the private sector and the Malaysian government.

Its recommendations include strengthening the Anti-Trafficking Law (Republic Act 9208), help for people deported from Malaysia, witness protection, better law enforcement and prosecution, and more public awareness.

books.title: Ukkil
books.subtitle: Visual Arts of the Sulu Archipelago
books.summary: The carved, woven and worked ornament of Sulu, ukkil, in a large illustrated study by the dancer and scholar who spent her life recording the archipelago’s arts.
books.overview:
Ligaya Fernando-Amilbangsa married into the family of the Sultan of Sulu and lived in the southern Philippines for more than 20 years. In this large illustrated book she records the visual arts of the Sulu archipelago, and argues that folk art should be read as a true record of social history.

The book has 7 chapters, one for each art: basketry, cloth weaving, embroidery, pottery, carving, blacksmithing and casting, and goldsmithing. She describes how each is made in close detail, from weaving looms to the oil used in casting, and links Sulu motifs such as the boat, the bird, the fish and the dragon to the rest of the Philippines and Asia. A reviewer in the Kyoto Review notes 2 full pages showing the parts of a Sama lepa houseboat.

She regrets the loss of some boats, carvings and crafts, and recommends reviving them. The book has photographs with long captions, a glossary and a bibliography. Ateneo de Manila University Press published it in 2005, and it was a finalist for the Gintong Aklat Award for the arts in 2006.

books.title: Pangalay
books.subtitle: Traditional Dances and Related Folk Artistic Expressions
books.summary: The pangalay dance of Sulu and the dances, music and dress around it, documented in the field by the woman who brought it to the national stage.
books.overview:
This book documents pangalay, the traditional dance of the Tausug, Sama, Badjao and Jama Mapun of the Sulu archipelago, together with related folk arts. It includes written instructions for performing the dances. It won the Manila Critics Circle award for best art book in 1983.

Ligaya Fernando-Amilbangsa first saw pangalay at a wedding in Jolo in 1969. She lived in the Sulu archipelago for about 30 years, taught at a Mindanao State University campus in Bongao and spent decades researching, practising and teaching the dance. She received the Ramon Magsaysay Award in 2015.

books.title: Space and Identity
books.subtitle: Expressions in the Culture, Arts and Society of the Muslims in the Philippines
books.summary: Moro art, architecture and ornament read for the ideas of space and self behind them, by a Tausug art historian.
books.overview:
Abraham P. Sakili's study looks at how the Muslims of the Philippines think about and use space, and uses that idea to read their visual arts, architecture and culture as a whole. It works mainly from the Muslims' own point of view, especially those of southern Mindanao, and has many colour pictures of works of art. The UP Asian Center published it in 2003, in 275 pages with a bibliography and index.

Sakili has also written on what he calls the "Mindanao problem", which he sees as rooted in history and culture, and on the torogan, the Maranao royal house.

books.title: Selected Essays on Mindanao Art and Culture
books.summary: Essays on the Indian and Islamic strands in Mindanao’s arts and epics, by a scholar of Sanskrit in the Philippines.
books.overview: Juan R. Francisco is a Filipino scholar of India and Sanskrit who taught at the University of the Philippines. He was the first to publish an English translation of Maharadia Lawana, the Maranao version of the Indian epic Ramayana. This volume gathers his essays on the art and culture of Mindanao, with attention to the Indian and Islamic strands in its arts and epics. Mindanao State University published it in 1988 as a special number of the Mindanao Journal (volume 14).

books.title: Moro Swords
books.summary: The kris, barong, kampilan and the rest, their forms, their making and their meaning, in the standard illustrated guide for collectors.
books.overview:
Robert Cato's illustrated book on Moro swords was published by Graham Brash in Singapore in 1996. A collector's review says it covers how the kris, kampilan and barong are made and where they come from, along with their sheaths, lesser-known swords, and the history of the popular Muslim weapons plaque.

Collectors on specialist forums note its influence on Moro sword collecting, though some question how carefully its claims were checked. Library records list a short bibliography.

books.title: Weapons of Moroland
books.summary: A collector’s illustrated catalogue of Moro blades and arms, printed on demand.
books.overview:
This illustrated book shows Moro weapons and other artefacts from the Philippines and the islands that traded with them. Each item appears in full-colour photographs with a short note on its size, materials and where it was found. The publisher says many of the pieces come from private collections in the Philippines and have not been shown in public before.

Its author, Bruce Jenkins, directs the Moroland Museum and is the author, publisher and main photographer of its book series. He made the book to document the museum's archives. It is the second volume of the series, after Krises of Moroland, and later volumes were planned on swords, daggers, shields, armour, bows and arrows. The 70-page book appeared on September 25, 2015.

The title echoes the "Weapons of Moroland" souvenir plaques, which display spears, shields and blades such as the kris, barong and kampilan.

books.title: Krises of Moroland
books.summary: A companion catalogue devoted to the kris, printed on demand.
books.overview:
Krises of Moroland is a picture book of krises and related artefacts from the Philippines and the islands that traded with them, drawn from private collections. It is the first volume of the Moroland Museum Historical Publications, a series planned to cover swords, daggers, shields, armour, bows and arrows. Each item is shown in full-colour photographs with a short note on its size, materials and where it was found. The publisher says many of the pieces have never been seen in public outside their owners' hands.

Its author, Bruce Jenkins, directs the Moroland Museum and is the series' author, publisher and main photographer. He says he made the books to document the museum's archives, and that he has visited the Philippines many times to see family and gather information. The 64-page book was printed on demand through CreateSpace on September 4, 2015.

books.title: Darangen
books.subtitle: In Original Maranao Verse, with English Translation
books.summary: The Maranao epic of Bantugan and the kingdom of Bembaran, sung for centuries around Lake Lanao, transcribed and translated in eight volumes by Mindanao State University; inscribed by UNESCO in 2005 as a masterpiece of oral heritage.
books.overview:
The Darangen is the epic of the Maranao of Lake Lanao. It runs to 17 cycles and some 72,000 lines, and is sung or chanted at weddings and celebrations. Its best-known stories follow the hero Bantugan and the kingdom of Iliyan a Bembaran.

Scholars of the Folklore Division of the Mindanao State University Research Center spent 10 years collecting it from Maranao elders and from kirim, handwritten Maranao songbooks in Arabic script, with support from the Toyota Foundation. The whole epic was published in 8 volumes from 1986 to 1988, in the original Maranao with an English translation. Hadji Lawa Cali and others transcribed and translated it, and Ma. Delia Coronel rendered the English in verse. Volume 1 opens with the story of the first ruler, Diwata Ndaw Gibon of Iliyan a Bembaran.

The Darangen was declared a National Cultural Treasure in 2002, and UNESCO proclaimed it a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity in 2005.

books.title: Stories from the Darangen
books.summary: Episodes of the Maranao epic retold in English prose, for readers who will not face the eight volumes.
books.overview:
Howard P. McKaughan compiled these stories from the Darangen, the Maranao epic, translated into English. De La Salle University Press published the book in 1995, at 194 pages. An earlier version was printed by the Mindanao State University research centre in Marawi. In the same year the press published a companion volume, Maranao Stories, and Connie Jan Maraan reviewed the 2 books together in the Philippine Journal of Linguistics in 1996.

McKaughan was an American linguist who founded the Department of Linguistics at the University of Hawaii. He died in 2013, aged 91. He also did fieldwork in the eastern highlands of New Guinea. His colleagues remembered him above all for his work on Maranao. With Batua Macaraya he compiled a Maranao dictionary. After retiring he worked with the Iranun people of Sabah for the Summer Institute of Linguistics.

books.title: Thirteen Tausug Folktales
books.summary: Tausug tales collected and translated by the university’s research centre.
books.overview:
This small book collects 13 Tausug folktales. It was published by the University Research Center of Mindanao State University in Marawi City as number 8 of its series Mindanao Art and Culture, and it runs to 106 illustrated pages.

Catalogues spell the title "Thirteen Tausog Folktales". A library record in Kedah, Malaysia, where a copy sits in the Ismail Hussein collection, names Raymond Llorca as editor. Library records give no date of publication, and none lists the 13 tales.

books.title: Voices from Sulu
books.subtitle: A Collection of Tausug Oral Traditions
books.summary: Tausug epics, tales, songs and sayings recorded over forty years in Sulu, with translations, from the founder of the journal Sulu Studies.
books.overview:
This 436-page collection gathers Tausug oral art recorded decades ago in the Sulu archipelago: stories, chants, poems, proverbs and riddles. The book credits the storytellers and singers as its real authors, among them Mullung (Muhammad Absari Salahuddin). Gerard Rixhon edited and compiled it for the Ateneo de Manila University Press's Mindanao Studies series.

Some pieces first appeared in the journal Sulu Studies. Others come from Tausug tales collected by the anthropologist H. Arlo Nimmo in the early 1960s. Rixhon and Nimmo annotate the texts and keep them close to their original form, even where they depart from mainstream Islamic teaching. The text is mostly in English, with some Tausug. Rixhon closes with an overview and classification of Tausug oral traditions.

books.title: Maranao Stories
books.summary: Maranao folktales translated into English, from the linguist who compiled the Maranao dictionary.
books.overview:
Howard P. McKaughan compiled this book of Maranao folktales translated into English. De La Salle University Press in Manila published it in 1995, at 141 pages, with a short bibliography. In the same year the press published a companion volume he compiled, Stories from the Darangen, drawn from the Maranao epic. Connie Jan Maraan reviewed the 2 books together in the Philippine Journal of Linguistics in 1996.

McKaughan was an American linguist who founded the Department of Linguistics at the University of Hawaii. He died in 2013, aged 91. He also did fieldwork in the eastern highlands of New Guinea. His colleagues remembered him above all for his work on Maranao. With Batua Macaraya he compiled a Maranao dictionary. After retiring he worked with the Iranun people of Sabah for the Summer Institute of Linguistics.

books.title: Mga Kuwentong Maranao
books.summary: Plays drawn from Maranao tales, written in Filipino by Frank Rivera for the Sining Kambayoka theatre of Mindanao State University.
books.overview:
This book collects plays by Frank G. Rivera for Sining Kambayoka, the folk theatre company he founded at Mindanao State University in Marawi in the 1970s. The plays drew on Maranao arts, such as the bayok chant and characters from old tales, and mixed them with comment on the politics of the day.

Arthur P. Casanova edited the collection, with an introduction by Anita M. Navarro. The UST Publishing House published it in 2003. Library records note texts in Filipino, English and Cebuano.

books.title: Tales from Lake Lanao and Other Essays
books.summary: Stories of the lake and essays on Maranao life by a Maranao anthropologist.
books.overview:
This collection by Nagasura T. Madale brings together essays on Maranao oral literature, Islamic literature and Philippine folklore. The National Commission for Culture and the Arts published it in Manila in 2001 as a first edition of 120 pages, with illustrations and references.

The library contents list opens with "The Great Tataro", then "Maranao Forms of Oral Literature", "Legends of the Maranao" and "A Preliminary Classification of Muslim Literature". Further pieces look at "The Role of Islamic Literature in the Development of the Wisdom of the Ummah", religion and culture from the Muslim-Filipino point of view, and the sarimanok as a symbol of national unity. Others treat the political uses of folklore, with the Malakas and Maganda creation story as the case, and there are pieces titled "Mother Earth" and "Sitti Maryam and Nabi Isa".

In the 1960s Madale, then a public school teacher, taught Maranao to the scholar Juan R. Francisco. He then worked as Francisco's research assistant on a study of Sanskrit elements in Maranao language and literature, the fieldwork that turned up the Maranao Ramayana tale Maharadia Lawana.

books.title: Children of the Ever-Changing Moon
books.subtitle: Young Moro Writers’ Anthology
books.summary: Essays by young Moro writers from across the region, the first anthology of its kind, edited by a Maguindanaon filmmaker.
books.overview:
This was the first anthology of essays by young Moro writers. Anvil published it in 2007, at 119 pages, and launched it on November 29 that year with Ambeth Ocampo, chairman of the National Historical Institute, as guest. Anvil's statement said the writers reflect on identity, religion, relationships, loss, tradition and change.

It was edited by Gutierrez "Teng" Mangansakan II, a Maguindanaon filmmaker and writer, who also wrote for it. The other 15 essayists were Ayesah Abubakar, Pearlsha Abubakar, Sarah Matalam-Alvarez, Mucha-Shim Quiling Arquiza, Nefertari Al-Raschid-Arsad, Allyson Banga-an, Ayesha Merdeka Alonto-Datu Ramos, Sittie Jamairah Disomimba, Samira Ali Gutoc, Sitti Djalia Turabin-Hataman, Loren Hallilah Lao, Zainudin Malang, Farida D. Mending, Gonaranao B. Musor and Sahara Alia Jauhali Silongan.

Ricardo de Ungria, a retired professor of UP Mindanao, looking back in 2025, finds in the essays conflicts between a traditional household and a modern daughter, the alienation of an uncommon name or way of praying, the need to prove oneself twice as worthy as a non-Moro, and women seeking a place at peace talks. Mangansakan followed it with Rays of the Invisible Light in 2015 and Panumtuman in 2024.

books.title: Notes on Bantugan’s Last Journey
books.summary: The kapagipat, the Maguindanaon crocodile ritual, and the Darangen as living memory: an ethnographic memoir from 25 years of fieldwork by a Maguindanaon filmmaker and writer.
books.overview:
Gutierrez Mangansakan II calls the book part ethnographic memoir, part field diary and part meditation. At its centre is the kapagipat, an old Maguindanaon ritual in which the crocodile, pagali or "relative", is a figure of passage between worlds. Around it are the music of the tagunggo, the tunung spirits of the unseen world, and the Darangen, which he treats not as an epic but as a living scripture of memory.

The book grew out of 25 years of research and fieldwork that began after the all-out war of 2000. It took him to the coastal villages of Maguindanao and the fishing communities of Cotabato, where the old stories survived displacement, religious intolerance and the erosion of memory. He writes that it is not about a culture preserved in amber but one that persists, changes, hides and resurfaces.

It is also, he says, a book about coming home to his identity as Maguindanaon and Moro. He announced it on his own site in August 2026.
books.note: The publisher, page count and ISBN have not been published yet.

books.title: Panitikang Mëranaw
books.summary: Maranao legends and tales, in Maranao and Filipino, for the Commission on the Filipino Language.
books.overview: Sandor B. Abad researched and gathered this collection of Maranao legends and stories, as its subtitle, Mga Piling Alamat at Kuwento (selected legends and tales), says. The texts are given in Maranao and in Filipino. Rogelio G. Mangahas and Roberto T. Añonuevo served as consultants and editors for the Filipino. The Komisyon sa Wikang Filipino published it in 2013 in its Aklat ng Bayan series.

books.title: Abduction of Princess Lawanen
books.subtitle: Darangen
books.summary: An episode of the Maranao epic retold in English by a Maranao author and published independently.
books.overview:
Nosca Khalid's book retells Episode 8 of the Darangen, the Maranao epic, in English. It is part of his series Darangen: Epic of the Maranaws and was published independently on March 16, 2017, at 131 pages. The episode tells how Princess Lawanen of the kingdom of Bembaran is carried off and recovered. It is one of the most often told parts of the epic.

In the book's description, Khalid writes that he could not imagine how his people produced such a work, and calls it the world's longest epic now that it is in English. He points to an episode in which a hero dives into the lake, lives a whole second life with a family elsewhere, and surfaces to find his wife still bathing, as an early story of time travel.

Khalid was born in Marawi City in 1952 and raised by his widowed mother. On a government scholarship for minorities he studied medicine and graduated in 1977 from the University of the East Ramon Magsaysay Memorial Medical Center. From 1980 he worked as a general practitioner in Saudi Arabia.

books.title: A Maranao Dictionary
books.summary: The standard Maranao–English dictionary, compiled by an American linguist and a Maranao lexicographer.
books.overview:
This dictionary has about 18,000 Maranao entries, most explained in 2 to 4 English words or phrases. A second part works from English back to the Maranao entries. More than 3,000 words are shown in example sentences with free English translations, and more than 700 Maranao plant names are matched to their scientific names. A short sketch of Maranao grammar helps users find the base forms of words.

It was compiled by the American linguist Howard P. McKaughan and Batua A. Macaraya, and published by the University of Hawaii Press in 1967.

books.title: A Maguindanaon Dictionary
books.subtitle: Maguindanaon–English, English–Maguindanaon
books.summary: The fullest Maguindanaon dictionary, by an Oblate missionary at Notre Dame University in Cotabato City.
books.overview:
Robert E. Sullivan, an Oblate of Mary Immaculate priest, compiled this 2-way dictionary of Maguindanaon, with one part from Maguindanaon to English and one from English to Maguindanaon. The Institute of Cotabato Cultures at Notre Dame University in Cotabato City published it in 1986, in 545 large-format pages.

Besides the word lists, the front of the book carries short guides to the language by other linguists. Eric Fleischman wrote "The Maguindanaon alphabet" and a 20-page account of how Maguindanaon verbs are inflected. Ronald Moe added "How to find verb roots", to help users look up verbs.

Later work leans on it. Ruth Stickney's Maguindanao Grammar Supplement of 2009 cites its chapters, and the Austronesian Basic Vocabulary Database takes its Maguindanaon word list from it.

books.title: Tausug–English Dictionary
books.subtitle: Kabtangan Iban Maana
books.summary: The standard Tausug–English dictionary, from the Summer Institute of Linguistics; second edition 1994.
books.overview:
This is a dictionary of Tausug, the language of Sulu, with English meanings. It was compiled and edited by Irene U. Hassan, Seymour A. Ashley and Mary L. Ashley.

The first edition came out in Jolo in 1975 through the Coordinated Investigation of Sulu Culture, as a joint project with the Bureau of Public Schools and the Summer Institute of Linguistics. One library record says its aim was to help the use of Tausug in education and cultural life. A second edition followed in 1994 from Notre Dame of Jolo College and the Summer Institute of Linguistics, as volume 6 of the Sulu Studies series. It runs to about 688 pages, with an index compiled by Malcolm S. Armour and a bibliography.

books.title: Lexicon of Classical Literary Maranao Words and Phrases
books.summary: The old literary Maranao of the darangen and the bayok, glossed by the Maranao scholar who co-wrote the dictionary.
books.overview:
This lexicon glosses in English the words and phrases of classical literary Maranao. It was compiled by Batua Al-Macaraya and Engracia M. Macaraya and published in Marawi City in 1993 by the University Research Center of Mindanao State University, with sponsorship from the Toyota Foundation of Japan. It runs to 384 pages, after 26 pages of front matter that include a short bibliography.

Batua A. Macaraya had worked on the language long before. With the American linguist Howard P. McKaughan he compiled A Maranao Dictionary, published by the University of Hawaii Press in 1967.

books.title: Bokabularyong Maranao–Filipino–English
books.summary: A three-way wordlist from the Commission on the Filipino Language.
books.overview: This is a wordlist of Maranao with its equivalents in Filipino (Tagalog) and English. It was published in Manila in 2003 by the Komisyon sa Wikang Filipino, the Commission on the Filipino Language, as a first edition of 152 pages.

books.title: Intensive Tausug
books.subtitle: A Pedagogical Grammar of the Language of Jolo, Philippines
books.summary: A full course in Tausug grammar for the serious learner.
books.overview:
Intensive Tausug is a course in the language of Jolo Island and nearby islands such as Pata, Marunggas, Tapul and Lugus, and the common language of the Sulu archipelago. Carl R. Galvez Rubino wrote it as either a self-study grammar or a classroom textbook. It aims to build the basic skills of listening, speaking, reading and writing.

The book has 20 lessons. Each is built around dialogues chosen for their grammar, themes or culture, and new vocabulary follows each dialogue. Rubino assumes that most learners already speak Tagalog or another Philippine language. So he focuses on where Tausug differs from Tagalog, rather than on features that would only seem strange to an English speaker. The book runs to over 400 pages, in English and Tausug, with indexes.

books.title: Tausug Reader
books.summary: Graded Tausug texts with glossaries, for learners who have the grammar.
books.overview: This reader of Tausug texts was written by Wilma A. Amil, Nurylyn M. Jupackal, Fahkriemar H. Limpasan and Peria S. Ledesma, and edited by the linguist R. David Zorc. Dunwoody Press of Springfield, Virginia, brought it out in 2011. It runs to 252 pages and includes a bibliography. Dunwoody had earlier published Intensive Tausug, a teaching grammar of the language of Jolo by Carl Rubino, in 2006.

books.title: Maranao Reader
books.summary: 36 news articles and essays in Maranao, each with an English translation, for learners of the language.
books.overview:
Maranao Reader is a book of 36 short reading passages in Maranao, each with an English translation at the back. Jason Lobel, a linguist of Philippine languages, prepared it, and Dunwoody Press of Hyattsville, Maryland, published it in 2009, with a preface and an introduction.

The passages are mostly essays and news-style articles of 2 or 3 pages, many about Islam and Maranao life. Titles include "Qur'an-Reading Contest in Lanao", "The Maranao Sultanates", "Maranao and Its Sister Languages", "Respect the Rules of War in Mindanao", "Islamic Banking", "The Head Scarf: Symbol of Freedom", "Is Islam a Violent Religion?", "The First Muslim to Fast in Outer Space" and "Blackout once again!". Others deal with Jabidah, EDSA and the Muslims, death customs, family values and Marawi as an Islamic city.

The same press published Maranao Dialogs and Drills, which Lobel edited, in the same year.

books.title: Maranao Dialogs and Drills
books.summary: Conversational Maranao in dialogues and drills.
books.overview:
Maranao Dialogs and Drills is a course book for intermediate learners of Maranao, or for people who already know another Philippine language such as Tagalog or Maguindanaon. It was written by Almahdi G. Alonto, Abdullah B. Adam and the linguist R. David Zorc, edited by Jason Lobel, and published in 2009 by Dunwoody Press of Hyattsville, Maryland.

It has 64 dialogues with English translations. They run from greetings, shopping at the market and travelling around Marawi to the coronation of a sultan, the kandori feast, weddings, Eid, Ramadan, the singkil dance, wearing a malong, brasswork, a death in the family, banking and working abroad. 22 drills follow on grammar: focus, aspect, negatives, particles, causative verbs and idioms.

An introduction describes the language and its spelling. It notes that Maranao has about 1 million speakers, mostly in Lanao del Sur and Lanao del Norte, varies little from place to place, and is the only Philippine language with an interpretation of the Qur'an. It also gives advice on custom and manners for visitors.

books.title: Maguindanao Grammar Supplement
books.summary: A grammar sketch of Maguindanaon for learners.
books.overview:
Maguindanao Grammar Supplement is a course grammar of Maguindanaon in 43 short lessons, for English speakers learning the language. Ruth Stickney adapted it from a Tagalog grammar supplement of 1987 by OMF International and the linguist R. David Zorc revised it for this second edition, adding notes and a list of references. Dunwoody Press of Hyattsville, Maryland, published it in 2009 as the first of its training books on Maguindanao.

The lessons move from the basic clause and question words to linkers, possessives and non-verbal clauses. Most of the book then works through the verb, its focus forms, causatives and abilitatives. Later lessons cover plurals, comparison, time expressions, emotions, commands, negatives and word-building affixes. Appendices follow.

In her preface Stickney says the book is not a full linguistic analysis but a tool for those studying the language. It draws on earlier work by Ron Moe and Eric Fleischman, and its reference list of older Maguindanaon studies goes back to Thomas Forrest's word list of 1779.

books.title: Diccionario Moro-Maguindanao-Español
books.summary: The Jesuit mission’s Maguindanaon–Spanish dictionary, the first for the language, compiled at Tamontaka. Out of copyright and free to read.
books.overview:
Father Jacinto Juanmartí, a Spanish Jesuit missionary, published this dictionary in Manila in 1892. In his note to the reader he says that no dictionary of Maguindanaon existed and that nothing had been printed in the language except recent catechisms. He built the dictionary only from the spoken word of the people, drawing on the many years he had lived among them. He admits it is incomplete and offers it as a base for others to build on.

The first part runs from Maguindanaon to Spanish and the second from Spanish to Maguindanaon. Entries mark words borrowed from Malay, Arabic and Sanskrit, and from the Maranao of Lake Lanao and the speech of Buayan and the upper Pulangi. For beginners, verbs are given in their active and passive forms, with notes on past and future. Juanmartí adds that most of the hill peoples along the Pulangi also understood Maguindanaon, so the dictionary would serve with them too.

books.title: A Grammar of the Maguindanao Tongue
books.subtitle: According to the Manner of Speaking It in the Interior and on the South Coast of the Island of Mindanao
books.summary: Juanmartí’s 1892 grammar translated into English for the American army by Captain C. C. Smith of the 14th Cavalry. Out of copyright and free to read.
books.overview:
This is an English translation of a short Spanish grammar of the Maguindanaon language by the Jesuit missionary Jacinto Juanmartí. Captain C. C. Smith of the 14th Cavalry translated it at Camp Overton, Mindanao, in 1905, to learn the language himself. The US War Department printed it in 1906.

In his preface Juanmartí says there were almost no written texts to work from, so he built the rules from years of listening to speakers, with help from Malay. He wrote it for missionaries who would follow him. Smith adds that the speech of the Maguindanaon of Cotabato and of the Maranao of the lake region are close enough for the grammar to serve both. It notes, for example, that the Maranao use r where the Maguindanaon prefer l.

The book covers letters and sounds, nouns, verbs active and passive, adverbs and prepositions, and lists of common phrases. It ends with a short vocabulary of English, Maguindanaon and Malay, on pages 65 to 80.

books.title: Islamic Identity, Postcoloniality, and Educational Policy
books.subtitle: Schooling and Ethno-Religious Conflict in the Southern Philippines
books.summary: Schools as a front in the Moro conflict: what public schooling meant to Muslim Filipinos, and what the madrasah offered instead. Second edition 2020.
books.overview:
This book is a historical and ethnographic study of a century of efforts to use schooling to absorb the Muslims of Mindanao and Sulu into the Philippine nation. Jeffrey Ayala Milligan argues that the region is a test case for using education policy to ease conflict between ethnic and religious groups.

In the 2020 second edition, the chapters move from education before colonial rule, to American schooling of Muslim Filipinos from 1898 to 1935, which he calls "pedagogical imperialism". They then look at alienation from schooling in Muslim Mindanao today and the Islamisation of education through the madrasah. The last chapters propose a way forward and a Bangsamoro philosophy of education based on what he calls "prophetic pragmatism".

books.title: A Madrasah General Education Program for Muslim Mindanao
books.summary: A proposal, from an MSU educator, for a madrasah curriculum that could be recognised by the state, decades before the ALIVE programme.
books.overview:
Lolita Junio Damonsong-Rodriguez sets out a general education programme for the madrasah, the Islamic schools of Muslim Mindanao. The 216-page book was published in 1992 by the Office of the Vice Chancellor for Research and Extension of the Mindanao State University System in Marawi City, with illustrations and a 12-page bibliography.

A 2001 policy paper on bringing the madrasah into the Philippine school system, by Helen de Castro and Maria Camila Luz Ginete, drew on the book for its account of how these schools work. Most teach Arabic and Islamic studies, above all Qur'an reading, usually in Arabic, and some add maths, science and health. A full course takes 12 years in 3 stages of 4 years each: Ibtida'i, I'dade and Thanawi. A school that offers all 12 years is a ma'ahad. Most madrasahs are run by their owners, a community group or a mosque body, and live on fees and gifts, sometimes from the Middle East. In 2001, the paper notes, the government still did not recognise them.

books.title: Philippine Muslim-Christian Dialogue
books.summary: Essays on what dialogue between Muslims and Christians in the Philippines has been and could be, edited by the philosopher-priest Leonardo Mercado with Maxwell Felicilda.
books.overview:
This short book on dialogue between Muslims and Christians in the Philippines was edited by Leonardo N. Mercado and Maxwell Felicilda. Divine Word Publications in Manila published it in 1993 as number 1 of the MMCD Papers, a series of the Movement for Muslim-Christian Dialogue. It looks at what such dialogue in the Philippines has been and what it could become. Library records file it under Muslims in the Philippines, conflict management and ethnic relations. It runs to 65 pages, with an index.

Mercado, born in Cebu in 1935 and ordained a priest of the Society of the Divine Word in Rome in 1964, is best known as a pioneer of Filipino philosophy. His Elements of Filipino Philosophy (1974) argued that such a philosophy has to be built from the shared culture and behaviour of the people. He kept working on relations between the faiths. In 1999 he co-edited, with Lilian Curaming, 100 Years of Filipino Muslim-Christian Relations for Silsilah Publications in Zamboanga City.

books.title: The Moro Rebellion and the Search for Peace
books.subtitle: A Study on Christian-Muslim Relations in the Philippines
books.summary: The conflict read as a problem of relations between Christians and Muslims, from the Silsilah Dialogue Movement in Zamboanga.
books.overview:
Hilario M. Gomez Jr.'s book, subtitled A Study on Christian-Muslim Relations in the Philippines, reads the Moro rebellion through the history of relations between Christians and Muslims. Library records list its main subjects as the Moro National Liberation Front, Muslim political activity in Mindanao, and the island's autonomy and independence movements. Silsilah Publications in Zamboanga City published it in 2000, in 303 pages with colour pictures, maps, a 15-page bibliography and an index.

Gomez, born in 1941, is a Protestant churchman who has worked on this subject for decades. His doctoral thesis, distributed by University Microfilms in 1977, was titled The Muslim Filipino Rebellion: Meaning and Challenges to the Mission and Ministry of the Christian Church in the Philippines. He later became a bishop of the United Church of Christ in the Philippines and, as bishop emeritus, a co-convenor with Archbishop Fernando Capalla and Aleem Aboali Cali of the Bishops-Ulama Conference, which brings Christian and Muslim religious leaders together for dialogue in Mindanao.

books.title: Liberalism and the Quest for Islamic Identity in the Philippines
books.summary: How the liberal state and the Moro search for an Islamic political identity have failed to meet, by a Filipino political scientist.
books.overview:
Kenneth E. Bauzon's study looks at how liberalism, as it grew in the West, has shaped the way the Muslims of the Philippines are studied and governed. He starts with the social sciences. He argues that the positivist and behaviourist methods that came out of the Enlightenment are mechanistic and reductive. He then uses the idea of the ummah, the Muslim community, to explain the "Moro Problem", while warning against blaming the conflict on religion.

The book has 10 chapters and a foreword by the historian Cesar Adib Majul, who calls it the first full treatment of the Islamic world view as a way to explain the Muslim movement. It was published in 1991 in Manila by Ateneo de Manila University Press and in Durham, North Carolina, by the Acorn Press, with Duke University's Islamic and Arabian Development Studies.

George Weightman, reviewing it in the Journal of Southeast Asian Studies in 1994, found the sources thorough but the book repetitive, and said readers need some grounding in philosophy, the sociology of knowledge and Islam.

books.title: Born in the Year 1900 and Other Stories
books.summary: Short stories by the Jolo-born writer best known for “The Chieftest Mourner”, still one of the most taught stories in Philippine classrooms, from the University of the Philippines Press.
books.overview:
This collection from the University of the Philippines Press brings together 13 stories by Aida Rivera-Ford, the author of "Love in the Cornhusks" and "The Chieftest Mourner". The stories span 100 years and a wide range of characters across the islands. They mix fiction with history and biography in a light, humorous style.

Rivera-Ford was born in Jolo, Sulu, and grew up in different parts of the Visayas and Luzon, as her father was a judge. She graduated from Silliman University in 1949, where she edited the literary magazine Sands and Coral. At the University of Michigan she won the Hopwood Award for fiction. She later taught at the University of Mindanao and Ateneo de Davao, and in 1980 founded the Learning Center of the Arts in Davao, now the Ford Academy of the Arts.

books.title: Collected Works
books.summary: Aida Rivera-Ford’s stories, essays and other writing gathered in one volume late in her long life in Davao.
books.overview:
Aida Rivera-Ford was born in Jolo, Sulu, in 1926 and spent her working life in Davao as a fiction writer, playwright and teacher. She founded the Ford Academy of the Arts, the first fine arts school in Mindanao, and died at 99. This volume, published in 2012, gathers her short stories in English.

Her earlier books include Now and at the Hour and Other Stories (1958) and Born in the Year 1900 and Other Stories (1997). Her plays appeared as Heroes in Love: Four Plays, and her last book was Oyanguren: The Forgotten Founder of Davao (2010).

books.title: Surveyors of the Liguasan Marsh
books.edition: Reissued as Green Sanctuary, Giraffe Books, 2003
books.summary: Enriquez’s first novel, set among land surveyors in the Liguasan Marsh of Maguindanao, country he knew as a young man. First published in Australia, it was reissued in the Philippines in 2003 as Green Sanctuary.
books.overview:
This is the first novel of Antonio R. Enriquez, a Zamboanga-born writer in English. It grew out of his short story "The Surveyor", first printed in the Philippines Free Press and set in Cotabato. A revised version of that story became a chapter of the novel.

The University of Queensland Press in Australia published the novel in 1981, as volume 16 of its Asian and Pacific Writing series. It won Enriquez the first of his 2 Palanca grand prizes for the novel. Writing in the Philippine Star, a fellow Zamboanga writer called it "sui generis, post-modern fiction" that "defies realistic convention, but remains compellingly and hauntingly real".
