He also saw it as early Enriquez, before martial law turned his later fiction toward advocacy.

A revised edition was printed in Cagayan de Oro in 1991. The book was later reissued as Green Sanctuary.

books.title: The Unseen War and Other Tales from Mindanao
books.summary: Stories of Mindanao’s wars and the people who live through them, by the Zamboanga novelist.
books.overview:
This collection of short stories by Antonio R. Enriquez was published by Giraffe Books in Quezon City in 1996, in 244 pages. An annotated bibliography of Mindanao resources describes the stories as set in the Zamboanga peninsula and Maguindanao, mostly in the Spanish colonial days of the 17th century. They deal with clashes of religion, tradition and custom, and with wars fought with spears, arrows and long knives between Moro and Christian warriors.

Enriquez was born in Zamboanga and grew up in the old city. He left university in Manila without a degree and did odd jobs, among them work with a surveying company in Cotabato that gave him the setting of his first novel, Surveyors of the Liguasan Marsh. During martial law in the 1970s he headed an information office and did research on the Yakan of Basilan, and saw the suffering of its tribal peoples in the war between Christian forces and Moro rebels. He won 2 Palanca grand prizes for the novel and the SEA Write Award in 2002, and died in 2014.

books.title: The Voice from Sumisip & Four Short Stories
books.summary: A novella named for the town of Sumisip in Basilan, with four short stories.
books.overview:
This 124-page book by the Zamboanga writer Antonio R. Enriquez pairs a novella, "The Voice from Sumisip", with 4 short stories. Giraffe Books in Quezon City published it in 2003.

The novella is set among the Yakan of Sumisip in Basilan, where Enriquez spent what he called his "most beautiful years". Its central figure is Professor Jose, a folklorist doing research in Yakan country under Marcos's martial law. Through him the reader sees the Yakan world, its shamans and rituals, besieged by violent forces that come under the banners of religion. Jose's exposure to Yakan rites and beliefs shakes his Christian faith and his trust in science, and he finds himself caught between 2 worlds.

The 4 stories, "The Turtle-Egg Hunter", "Gatherer of the People", "Iba the Christian" and "Jainal the Pirate", go back to Naawan, the old name of Zamboanga, at the time of its founding. Francis Macansantos, reviewing the book in The Philippine Star in 2004, said they read like eyewitness accounts. He also noted that Enriquez had won the SEA Write Award for fiction in 2002.

books.title: The White Horse of Alih and Other Stories
books.summary: Stories by the Zamboanga writer. In the title story a Moro man, Alih, and his brother Omar plan to attack a crowd celebrating an American holiday, and Alih turns on his brother to stop him.
books.overview:
Mig Alvarez Enriquez, born in 1925, was a writer from Zamboanga City whose short stories won Palanca Awards. This collection was published by New Day Publishers in Quezon City in 1985.

The title story is set on 4 July, as a town celebrates an American holiday with a parade. Alih, a young Moro, and his older brother Omar plan an attack on the crowd. The white horse of the title comes from a belief that a Moro who kills and is killed in the act will be carried to paradise on a white horse. Readers have taken the story as one of shame, honour and redemption, and of prejudice based on race and religion.

Ma. Teresa Padilla reviewed the book in the journal Philippine Studies in 1987.

books.title: Three Philippine Epic Plays
books.subtitle: Lam-ang, Labaw Donggon and Bantugan
books.summary: Three epic heroes put on stage, among them Bantugan, the hero of the Maranao Darangen.
books.overview:
Mig Alvarez Enriquez turns 3 Philippine epics into plays, each in 3 acts. "Lam-ang, Son of Namongan" adapts a version of the Ilocano epic Biag ni Lam-ang. "Labaw Donggon, or the Hero Who Learned a Lesson" adapts a fragment of the Visayan epic Hinilawod. "Bantugan, or How Bantugan Married Fifty Women" adapts a fragment of the Darangen, the Maranao epic, whose hero Bantugan comes from Bumbaran. That play is dedicated to Al Glang, a Maguindanao scholar.

The Labaw Donggon play opens with an introduction to the epic that draws on Jocano. In a note, the playwright explains the form he calls total theater: instead of a curtain rising and falling on each scene, one scene ends as the next begins. He adds that the plays can also be staged as straight dramas.

Enriquez first learned theater arts from the Jesuits of the Ateneo de Zamboanga. He signed the preface in November 1982, and New Day Publishers of Quezon City brought the book out in 1983. His Two Liberation Plays of 1991 lists them as a trilogy.

books.title: Mindanao Harvest 4
books.subtitle: A 21st Century Literary Anthology
books.summary: An anthology of writing from Mindanao this century, edited at MSU-Iligan Institute of Technology, with Moro writers among its contributors, Calbi A. Asain’s story “Hegira” among them.
books.overview:
This anthology gathers new writing from and about Mindanao. It is edited by Jaime An Lim, Christine F. Godinez-Ortega and Ricardo M. de Ungria and was published by Far Eastern University, with a copyright date of 2019. It has 346 pages of poetry, fiction, essays and drama by 63 writers, most of them from the younger generation.

The editors meant it to help students understand Mindanao's 3 main peoples: the Lumad, the Moro, and the descendants of Christian settlers, now in their 3rd and 4th generations. Some pieces were written in English or Filipino. Others are translations into English or Filipino from Binukid, Maranao, Maguindanao and Mandaya.

The book is a sequel to Mindanao Harvest 1 and 2, published in 1995 and 1996. Mindanao Harvest 3, put together by Godinez-Ortega alone, was a book of folktales retold by 16 writers. Volume 4 was launched during the Diyandi Festival of Iligan City and later in Manila and Davao City. It won the National Book Award for best anthology in 2022.

books.title: Panunggud and Other Stories
books.summary: Stories of Tausug life in Sulu by a Tausug writer of fiction, from De La Salle University Press.
books.overview:
Panunggud and Other Stories is a collection of short stories in English by Calbi A. Asain, a Tausug writer from Sulu. De La Salle University Press published it in 2001, at 110 pages.

Asain has also written about Tausug oral literature. In a 2006 article in The Journal of History he described the parang sabil kissa, sung ballads and epics of Jolo that are meant both to entertain and to teach, sung by a woman playing the gabbang, a bamboo xylophone, often with a man on the biyula, a native violin.

His second collection, Bride Price and Other Stories, came out from Xavier University Press in 2023. Its publisher presents it as a book about the people of the Sulu archipelago and as part of a growing body of written Tausug literature.

books.title: With the Bravest
books.subtitle: The Untold Story of the Sulu Freedom Fighters of World War II
books.summary: The Tausug guerrillas who fought the Japanese in Sulu, told by a physician who was the youngest commander in the Sulu Area Command in 1945.
books.overview:
Ernesto M. Espaldon (1926 to 2006) joined the guerrillas of the Sulu Area Command at 16, during the Japanese occupation. The book's front matter names him the youngest commander in the Sulu Area Command in 1945. After the war he became a surgeon and settled in Guam, where he later served as a senator.

This is his account of the guerrilla resistance in Sulu during the Second World War, in which, as one description puts it, Muslim and Christian Filipinos fought side by side. Library records file it under personal narratives of the war and underground movements in the Sulu archipelago. It was published in 1997 by the Espaldon-Virata Foundation and distributed by Ateneo de Manila University Press, with a foreword by President Fidel V. Ramos.

books.title: The Songs of Salanda and Other Stories of Sulu
books.summary: Stories of the Sama Dilaut of Tawi-Tawi, written by the anthropologist who lived among them, from what he saw and was told.
books.overview:
This is a collection of 16 short stories by H. Arlo Nimmo, an anthropologist who spent 2 years in the mid-1960s among the Sama Dilaut, also called Bajau, of the Sulu archipelago. The Sama Dilaut were then nomadic boat-dwellers who lived in small family houseboats in the far south of the Philippines.

The stories are based on people, places and events Nimmo met during that fieldwork. Together they follow a young man coming of age among people unlike any he had known. The publisher calls it a personal look back at his first fieldwork, and a picture of a people and their culture on the edge of great change.

The University of Washington Press published it in 1994. A coloured map of the Sulu archipelago is printed on the endpapers.
books.blurb: In this engrossing collection of sixteen short stories, H. Arlo Nimmo tells of a young man coming of age while living among a remote cluster of islands in the southern Philippines with a people unlike any he had known. Nimmo combines an anthropologist's eye for the significant detail with a storyteller's gift for bringing his characters to life. His book is a vivid narrative of a people and their culture on the brink of momentous change. The Songs of Salanda is Nimmo's deeply personal exploration of his early anthropological field experiences in the Sulu archipelago. During two years in the mid-1960s, he researched the culture of the Bajau, a small group of nomadic boat-dwellers who plied the waters off the southernmost Philippine islands in small single-family houseboats. Nimmo's stories are based on the people, places, and events he encountered.

books.title: The Battle of Bayang and Other Essays on Moroland
books.summary: Essays on the history of the Moro South, the title essay on the 1902 battle in which American troops stormed the Maranao forts at Bayang, Lanao.
books.overview:
This short book collects 6 essays on the history of the Moro South by the sociologist Federico V. Magdalena. The Mamitua Saber Research Center of Mindanao State University published it in Marawi in 2002, to mark the centenary of the Battle of Bayang. In that battle, in Lanao in 1902, American troops fought the Maranao. Magdalena had read a paper, "Revisiting the 1902 Battle of Bayang", at the centenary in Marawi City that May.

The title essay on the battle comes first. It is followed by an essay on the American operations around Lake Lanao in 1902 and 1903, one on the Moro cotta, or fort, and a profile of the American officer Robert E. Lee Bullard (1861 to 1947). The last 2 essays move to later times: "Moros, Filipinos, and Americanos" and "Moro autonomy and the 1989 plebiscite".

Magdalena wrote widely on the Moros in the same years, on topics such as Moro resistance in the Philippine Revolution, the Chinese in Moroland, Islamic education, and John J. Pershing and the Lake Lanao datus.

books.title: The Muslim Filipinos
books.summary: A reader of essays on the history, faiths and cultures of the Muslim peoples of the Philippines, edited by the Maranao anthropologist.
books.overview:
The Muslim Filipinos: A Book of Readings was edited by Nagasura T. Madale and published by Alemar-Phoenix in Quezon City in 1981. It runs to 376 pages, with a bibliography of nearly 20 pages and an index. Library records list the civilisation of the Muslim peoples of the Philippines as its subject.

The book gathers essays by several writers. Among them is Eric Casiño's 1973 study "Politics, Religion, and Social Stratification: The Case of Cagayan Sulu". Later scholars still cite the reader. Patricia Horvatich, for example, draws on it for how older Philippine schoolbooks treated Muslim children, including lessons on raising pigs.

Madale wrote widely on Maranao folklore and literature. In the 1960s, as a public school teacher, he taught Maranao to the scholar Juan R. Francisco and became his research assistant. By the 1980s he was writing on the Moro separatist movement from Mindanao State University.

books.title: Possibilities for Peace in Southern Philippines
books.summary: A Maranao scholar’s reading of the conflict in the South and of what peace between its peoples would take, from the Silsilah Dialogue Movement.
books.overview: Nagasura T. Madale, a Maranao scholar, wrote the title essays of this book with other contributors. Its full title is Possibilities for Peace in Southern Philippines: The Islamic Concept of Peace and Other Essays. It was published in Zamboanga City by Silsilah Publications, the press of the Silsilah Dialogue Movement, which works for dialogue between Muslims and Christians. Library records date it to about 1990 or 1991. The essays take up the Islamic idea of peace and what peace between the peoples of the South would require, and include references.

books.title: Advancing Bangsamoro Aspirations
books.summary: Writings by the founder of the Institute of Bangsamoro Studies on the Bangsamoro’s road to self-determination: its history, the law and politics of the peace process, and what it means for peacebuilding elsewhere. Published for the 10th anniversary of the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro.
books.overview:
This book gathers 15 articles and speeches by Abhoud Syed M. Lingga, written between 2002 and 2016. They were given at forums in Geneva, Davao City, Penang, Khon Kaen, Cotabato City, Manila and Tirana, or printed in books such as Moro Reader and Mindanao Horizons. Topics run from the Bangsamoro right to self-determination and a referendum as a political option, to the role of third parties in the peace process, policing, and building the Bangsamoro government.

Lingga was part of the MNLF in Northern Mindanao in the 1970s, later co-founded the Institute of Bangsamoro Studies, and sat on the MILF peace panel that negotiated the Framework Agreement and the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro. The introduction notes that his early pieces focus on historical injustice, while the later ones look more closely at legal and political frameworks and community-based peacebuilding.

The Institute of Bangsamoro Studies and the Centre for Peace and Conflict Studies published it in September 2024, with funding from Misereor. It opens with forewords by MILF peace implementing panel chair Mohagher Iqbal and Emma Leslie, and closes with an essay by Robert Maulana Alonto.
books.note: Published with the Centre for Peace and Conflict Studies.

books.title: Peace is for Everyone
books.subtitle: Bangsamoro Stories of Hope, Survival, Pain and Resilience
books.summary: The stories of almost 300 Bangsamoro men and women, from Maguindanao, the Lanao provinces, the Zamboanga peninsula, Basilan, Sulu and Tawi-Tawi, of decades of conflict and their hopes after the 2014 peace agreement.
books.overview:
This book gathers the testimonies of almost 300 Bangsamoro men and women from Maguindanao, Cotabato, Sultan Kudarat, the 2 Lanao provinces, the Zamboanga peninsula, Basilan, Sulu and Tawi-Tawi, and the cities of Marawi, Iligan, Cotabato and Isabela. Many are survivors of massacres during the Mindanao conflict. A team from the Institute of Bangsamoro Studies, led by Abhoud Syed M. Lingga, did the interviews.

It uses a "peace history" approach, weaving single stories into a shared account. Its 5 chapters move from memories of living in harmony with settlers, through displacement, the Ilaga attacks, martial law and war, to what peace means to the speakers. A section of stories "we cannot forget" and a timeline close the book.

The foreword is by Mo Bleeker, who chaired the Transitional Justice and Reconciliation Commission. She notes that many speakers welcomed the 2014 peace agreements and saw self-government as a way to regain dignity.
books.note: Published with the Institute of Bangsamoro Studies.

books.title: Negotiating Peace
books.subtitle: An Insider’s Perspective on the Bangsamoros’ Struggle for Self-Determination
books.summary: The speeches of the MILF’s chief negotiator from 2005 to 2018, which follow the peace process with the government through the eyes of the Front.
books.overview:
This first volume gathers the speeches of Mohagher Iqbal, the Moro Islamic Liberation Front's chief negotiator, from 2005 to 2018. It was published by the Centre for Peace and Conflict Studies in Cambodia with funding from Norway's foreign ministry. Read in order, the speeches follow the talks between the government and the MILF from the exploratory talks in Kuala Lumpur to the years after the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro.

The book has 9 chapters, arranged by year: 2005 to 2010 in one chapter, then one chapter for each year from 2011 to 2018. It ends with a list of milestones in the peace process. Most pieces are opening and closing statements at the negotiating table, along with public speeches.

The foreword is by Emma Leslie, who sat in the International Contact Group that supported the talks. She describes Iqbal's careful preparation and his grasp of history, and calls the collection a historical record of a people's wish to have past injustices recognised and to govern themselves. An epigraph sums up Iqbal's stand: the right to self-determination cannot be negotiated, but the way to achieve it can.
books.note: Volume 1, 2005 to 2018.

books.title: Beyond the Peace Table
books.subtitle: Reflections on the GPH-MILF Peace Process
books.summary: Malaysia’s facilitator of the government–MILF talks on how they reached the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro in 2014, and how he got the two sides past their deadlocks.
books.overview:
Dato' Tengku Abdul Ghafar was the Malaysian diplomat who facilitated the talks between the Government of the Philippines and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front. He took part from 2000 to 2003, came out of retirement in 2011, and stayed until the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro was signed in March 2014. He died in September 2016, and this short book was published the next year by the Centre for Peace and Conflict Studies in Cambodia.

His own reflections come first. They cover Malaysia's part in the talks, the role of a facilitator, the negotiating panels and how the talks were structured, and the state of the peace process after the agreement. The introduction traces the conflict from the 1970s, the MNLF-MILF split and the Framework Agreement of 2012.

The second half is tributes from people who worked with him, including MILF chief negotiator Mohagher Iqbal and government panel chair Miriam Coronel-Ferrer. A foreword by his son opens the book.

books.title: The Journey of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front’s First Ex-Combatants
books.summary: Interviews with 10 of the 145 MILF fighters who handed in their weapons at the first decommissioning, in Sultan Kudarat, Maguindanao, in June 2015, on the lives they hoped to build.
books.overview:
On 16 June 2015, at the old Capitol Building in Sultan Kudarat, Maguindanao, 145 combatants of the Bangsamoro Islamic Armed Forces were registered in the first phase of MILF decommissioning, under the Annex on Normalisation of the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro. In late July the MILF invited the Centre for Peace and Conflict Studies to interview 10 of them.

The book sets out what these men said, in 7 short chapters named after their own words, from "The conflict disturbed our lives" to "We are still waiting for the assistance to come, for our lives to change" and "It is peacetime now". They talk about the war, memories of the struggle, their commitment to the peace process and their hopes for civilian life. The preface says the aim was to help them move from a story of conflict to a story of peace, and argues that decommissioning is a means to a different life, not an end in itself.

Nerea Bilbatúa conceived and wrote the book, with photographs by Toto Lozano and Karlos Manlupig. The British Embassy in Manila funded it.

books.title: Marawi
books.subtitle: Rebuilding from Ashes to a City of Faith, Hope and Peace
books.summary: What the survivors of the 2017 siege of Marawi told listeners about their losses, life in the evacuation centres and the city they want rebuilt.
books.overview:
This report records what survivors of the 2017 siege of Marawi said in conversations with trained local "listeners" from January to March 2018. The listeners spoke with 1,133 people, most of them displaced, in evacuation centres and host homes. The Centre for Peace and Conflict Studies ran the project with Dansalan College, Mindanao State University and the Institute of Bangsamoro Studies.

Chapter 1 gives the setting and a summary of findings and recommendations. Chapter 2 sets out the community accounts: the siege itself, life as displaced people, and views on the government, the military and the ISIS-Maute group. Chapter 3 explains the listening method.

Survivors spoke of poor relief food, favouritism in aid, crowded evacuation centres, children out of school and weak health care. Many wanted work, money to restart their businesses and a safe return home. Some feared losing their land because deeds were lost or because Marawi was declared a military reservation in 1953.

books.title: The Role of Trust in Peace Accord Implementation
books.subtitle: A Case Study in the Bangsamoro
books.summary: A community survey on what trust means to people living with the government–MILF peace accords, what builds it and what wears it down, with advice for the parties and those carrying the accords out.
books.overview:
This learning paper asks how trust can be kept alive once a peace accord has been signed. It is an abridged version of the author's master's thesis at the Centre for Peace and Conflict Studies in Cambodia. Fred Lubang is a Mindanao peace builder who led the Philippine Campaign to Ban Landmines and worked from Cotabato City on a 2010 government–MILF agreement to clear explosive remnants of war.

The study draws on that clearance work. Lubang interviewed members of both peace panels, the International Monitoring Team and other key actors, and surveyed 2 communities in Maguindanao, one already cleared of unexploded ordnance and one still waiting. The paper defines trust at the level of the person, the group and society, then sets out survey results, interview findings and recommendations.

It finds that transparency, open communication and a "leap of faith" matter most to people in conflict areas, while insincerity, doubt and unkept promises wear trust down.

books.title: Resolving Conflict in Muslim Mindanao
books.subtitle: Showcasing Four Traditional Methods
books.summary: Four ways Moro communities settle disputes and feuds by custom, set out by researchers from those communities, with the case for building them into the formal justice system.
books.overview:
This book gathers 4 studies of how disputes are settled in Muslim Mindanao outside, or alongside, the ordinary courts. Each researcher grew up with the tradition they describe. It was published by the Institute of Bangsamoro Studies in Cotabato City with the Centre for Peace and Conflict Studies in Cambodia.

Abubakar Datumanong, a grandson of the 23rd Sultan of Maguindanao, writes on the role of Maguindanaon datus in settling conflict. Parido Rahman Pigkaulan sets out Islamic principles of conflict resolution and how the Shari'ah courts and the Agama Arbitration Council work, arguing that they help ease congestion in the regular courts. Maguid Makalingkang surveys people in Maguindanao on which of 4 mechanisms they prefer and find effective: traditional settlement, the Shari'ah circuit court, the municipal trial court and the Katarungang Pambarangay. Juwairiya Uka-Lingga documents traditional conflict resolution among the Teduray of Upi.

The introduction argues that these customary methods deserve recognition and a place within formal justice and peacebuilding.
books.note: Published with the Centre for Peace and Conflict Studies.

books.title: Embedding Feedback Mechanisms
books.subtitle: Bringing Voices from the Ground to the GPH-MILF Peace Talks
books.summary: A way to carry what the victims of violence in Mindanao say up to the negotiators at the government–MILF peace talks.
books.overview:
This is an action research study by Elizabeth M. Padilla, completed in November 2011 for the Applied Conflict Transformation Studies course. It follows her organisation, Sustainable Alternatives for the Advancement of Mindanao (SALAM), as it tried to pass the concerns of people hurt by violence in their communities to the government and MILF negotiating panels.

The work ran in 3 cycles: planning with SALAM staff and its board, dialogues and focus groups with community residents, and a consultation with the MILF peace panel. Background chapters cover theories of change and peacebuilding, and the all-out war of 2000 and the MILF attacks of 2008.

The findings are lessons for the organisation. An organisation needs to be clear about its role. Constructive communication helps bring change. Spaces to exchange views build trust. Letting people state their needs can free them. Accepting limits can itself drive change. The paper ends with recommendations. It was published by the Centre for Peace and Conflict Studies.

books.title: Perspectives of the Subanen Tribe on the New Bangsamoro Political Entity
books.summary: What the Subanen, an indigenous people of the Zamboanga peninsula who are not Muslim, thought of the Bangsamoro entity then being negotiated, and what they asked of it.
books.overview:
This study, prepared for a 2013 peace practitioners' research conference, asked how much the Subanen of Zamboanga del Sur and Zamboanga Sibugay know of their old kinship with the Moros, and whether that shapes their view of the new Bangsamoro political entity. The authors are Mindanao State University and Cotabato City State Polytechnic College lecturers working with the Institute of Bangsamoro Studies.

The researchers used a survey of 324 Subanen, key informant interviews and focus groups. About 55% of respondents had little knowledge of Moro and Subanen kinship. Most gave the new entity low support, and those who knew less of the kinship supported it less.

The authors conclude that the Subanen hope for a peaceful end to the conflict but offer no plan of their own, and are mostly content with the status quo. They warn that the old partnership between the 2 peoples is weakening.
books.note: A paper for the 2013 Peace Practitioners’ Research Conference; the authors wrote it at the Institute of Bangsamoro Studies.

books.title: Transition to the Bangsamoro
books.subtitle: Change and Imagination
books.summary: A 326-page collection published a year after the 2012 Framework Agreement on the Bangsamoro, on the move from the ARMM to a new Bangsamoro political entity. Edited by IAG founder Benedicto Bacani, with contributions including Peter Koeppinger, Crisanto Cayon and Kathleen Geslani.
books.overview: This 326-page book was published by the Institute for Autonomy and Governance (IAG) in Cotabato City in 2013, a year after the Framework Agreement on the Bangsamoro. IAG describes it as a special issue of its journal that invited readers to imagine the future of the Bangsamoro, as the region prepared to move from the ARMM to a new political entity. It was edited by Benedicto Bacani, IAG's founder and executive director, who also gave technical help to the Bangsamoro Transition Commission that drafted the Bangsamoro Basic Law.

books.title: Looking Back, Moving Forward
books.subtitle: Gains, Challenges and Opportunities for Civil Society Participation in Bangsamoro Governance
books.summary: A study of how civil society organisations take part in politics and governance in the new BARMM during the transition period. It takes stock of what civil society has gained, the obstacles it faces in dealing with leaders and institutions, and where it can do more.
books.overview:
This study by the Institute for Autonomy and Governance looks at what civil society organisations in the Bangsamoro do and how much say they have in government during the move from the ARMM to the BARMM. It was part of the EU-funded DELACSE Bangsamoro project with Konrad Adenauer Stiftung. Starjoan Villanueva did the research and writing.

The research is qualitative. It rests on 58 interviews done in late 2019: 44 with leaders of organisations picked at random from a list of more than 90, and 14 more with coalitions, a think tank, members of the Bangsamoro Transition Authority and a former woman legislator from Tawi-Tawi. Chapters profile the organisations, their programmes and areas of work, the quality of their participation, women's political participation, the obstacles and the openings.

It finds a lively and growing civil society that works best at barangay, municipal and provincial level, and is weakest at policy advocacy and monitoring at regional level. It points to the codes the Bangsamoro Parliament must pass as one place for organisations to take part.

books.title: Research on Traditional Madaris in ARMM and Adjacent Regions
books.summary: A baseline study of the traditional madrasah system in the ARMM and nearby regions, funded by the Australian Government. It gathers data meant to guide public policy on traditional madaris and on the education system of the new BARMM.
books.overview:
The Institute for Autonomy and Governance in Cotabato City carried out this study, with Australian Government funding. It looks at traditional madaris: private Islamic schools that operate outside the Philippine school system. The team took a census of 1,850 traditional madaris, surveyed 169 of them, held 6 focus groups and interviewed 21 people from government, universities, civil society and the security sector.

It counts at least 1,534 traditional madaris in the ARMM and 316 in nearby regions. Most teach at the kindergarten and primary levels, and only 2% offer college. The study finds that the schools live on donations and volunteer work, and have no access to public funds because they are not accredited. About 90% of madrasah leaders want government recognition. Graduates have few jobs open to them. Leaders are worried by the growing view that madaris are used for recruitment by extremist groups.

The chapters trace the history of madrasah education, the state of the schools, their problems and proposals for the future, including a vision for education in the Bangsamoro. An annex lists the madaris surveyed.

books.title: Research on Youth Vulnerability to Violent Extremism in the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao
books.summary: A survey-based study, done with the Centre for Humanitarian Dialogue, of how vulnerable young people in the ARMM are to violent extremism. It aims to give government agencies and communities an early picture to shape their response.
books.overview:
This study by the Institute for Autonomy and Governance asks how open young Muslims in the ARMM are to radicalisation and recruitment. It covers Maguindanao, Lanao del Sur, Basilan and Sulu. The team surveyed 100 young people, held focus groups with youth leaders and ulama, interviewed 35 key informants and wrote 4 case studies of young people who had been in violent groups.

The 7 chapters cover the method, the history of extremism in Mindanao, the study sites, young people's views of Islam, their views on extremist groups and recruitment, and ideas for prevention.

The study found no large-scale radicalisation. Most young people knew basic Islamic teaching but little of the ideas extremists use. Only a minority sympathised with extremist groups, and far more feared them. Many named the loss of family and community ties as the worst effect.

books.title: Youth Vulnerability to Violent Extremism
books.subtitle: A Follow-through Study in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao
books.summary: A follow-up to IAG's 2017 study that tracks how urban Bangsamoro youth's views and attitudes toward violent extremism have changed. It adds the views of young people living in conflict-affected rural areas of the BARMM.
books.overview:
The Institute for Autonomy and Governance (IAG) released a study of urban Moro youth and violent extremism in 2017, as the Marawi siege unfolded; that study fed into the government's national action plan on preventing violent extremism. This follow-up asks what changed after the Bangsamoro Organic Law, the new MILF-led government, the Taliban's return and the Anti-Terrorism Act of 2020.

The team surveyed 800 young people: 400 in Cotabato City, Marawi City, Lamitan City and Jolo, and 400 in conflict-affected rural areas of Mamasapano, Butig, Patikul and Tipo-Tipo. They also held 32 key informant interviews and 24 focus groups, and wrote 5 case studies of former members of the Abu Sayyaf, Maute group and BIFF. Chapters cover knowledge of Islamic concepts, recruitment, prevention programmes, a comparison with 2017, and suggestions from stakeholders.

Most respondents held mainstream views of Islam. One exception stood out: 50.4% agreed that armed jihad is an obligation of every Muslim, the reading spread by extremist groups.

books.title: Balik-Islam in the Philippines
books.summary: A study, done with the UP Institute of Islamic Studies, of Filipinos who convert or 'revert' to Islam, building a profile of converts and their reasons for conversion. It also gathers Muslim and non-Muslim opinions on Islam and looks at converts' links to violent extremist groups.
books.overview:
This study looks at Balik-Islam, Filipinos who convert or "revert" to Islam. Many embraced Islam while working in the Middle East. It was done by the Institute for Autonomy and Governance with the University of the Philippines Institute of Islamic Studies, with funding from the Australian Embassy. Reports that some converts had joined violent extremist groups prompted the research, which asks how vulnerable converts are and what government and other groups should do.

The team surveyed 80 converts in the BARMM and 109 in Luzon and Metro Manila, and held 8 focus groups, more than 40 key informant interviews, interviews with 3 persons deprived of liberty, and 9 case studies. Chapters cover who the converts are, why they converted, the difficulties they face, their views on Islam, non-Muslims and armed groups, and the services they need.

Most respondents saw groups like the Abu Sayyaf, Maute and ISIS as distorting Islam. The study found that many converts are jobless or poor, and that discrimination is their main problem, one that could leave them more open to extremism.

books.title: Empowering Madaris in the BARMM through Public Policy and Regional Autonomy to Help Prevent and Counter Violent Extremism
books.summary: A study of how vulnerable or resilient the madrasah system is to violent extremism, and where it is heading in the Philippines. It weighs how public policy and the BARMM's regional autonomy can support madrasah development.
books.overview:
This 2023 study by the Institute for Autonomy and Governance asks how far madaris in the BARMM are open to, or protected against, recruitment by violent extremist groups. It also looks at where madrasah education is heading and what public policy and regional autonomy can do for it. The Australian Government funded it.

The researchers surveyed 198 madrasah heads and senior teachers, interviewed 7 regional and local officials, and held focus groups with 44 stakeholders in the 5 BARMM provinces. Key informants saw brighter prospects: a Directorate General on Madrasah Education now has a budget, and the Bangsamoro Education Code provides for public madaris run by the Ministry of Basic, Higher and Technical Education. But 7 in 10 of those surveyed said that being near conflict zones, and the presence of extremist groups, make schools vulnerable. They also pointed to limited funding and weak government oversight.

The report has chapters on the literature, method and findings, and ends with recommendations on policies and programmes.

books.title: Research on the Implementation of the National Action Plan on Preventing and Countering Violent Extremism (NAP P/CVE) in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao
books.summary: An assessment of how the national plan against violent extremism is being carried out in the 5 provinces of the BARMM. It draws on interviews with 50 officials, 10 focus groups with 78 community leaders and a survey of 150 programme beneficiaries.
books.overview:
This report by the Institute for Autonomy and Governance looks at how the National Action Plan on Preventing and Countering Violent Extremism is carried out in the BARMM. Its 5 chapters cover the background, a review of the literature and laws, the method, the findings and the recommendations. The Australian Government funded it.

National agencies, the regional government and civil society viewed the plan well, and praised its local version under the Bangsamoro Task Force for Ending Local Armed Conflict. But only 40% of programme beneficiaries had heard of the national plan. 98% said the programmes they joined helped prevent extremism. Beneficiaries also complained of no follow-up support and of bias in choosing who got help.

The main recommendation is a regional system to monitor and evaluate these programmes, with a public database. The report also calls for programmes suited to each province's needs and culture.

books.title: Setting Baselines
books.subtitle: Preparing the BARMM Electorate for the First Ever Regional Parliamentary Elections in 2025
books.summary: A survey report on the voters of the BARMM ahead of its first regional parliamentary elections. It profiles likely voters, how ready they are for the polls, where they get news of political parties, and the issues that drive their choices.
books.overview:
The Institute for Autonomy and Governance (IAG) surveyed 3,072 likely voters across the BARMM from 29 April to 14 May 2024, a year before the region's first parliamentary elections. This report sets out what they found. Its chapters profile likely voters, measure how ready they are for the polls, trace where they hear about political parties, list what voters want and why they would back a party, and close with opportunities and the survey method.

Most voters knew little about the new system. 58.4% said they knew nothing of it and 24% very little, and nearly 9 in 10 knew little about the party-list, district and sectoral seats of the 80-member parliament. Family and friends, social media and barangay officials were the main sources of news; print barely figured. Livelihood projects, education, jobs, and peace and order topped voters' concerns, well ahead of violent extremism.

The report urges COMELEC, the Bangsamoro Electoral Office and civil society to run voter education through social media, radio and local languages, using pictures and video over text.

books.title: The Indigenous Peoples of Mainland ARMM
books.subtitle: A Brief Socio-cultural, Economic, and Demographic Profile of the Teduray, Lambangian, Dulangan Manobo and Higaonon Societies in the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao
books.summary: A short profile of the non-Moro indigenous peoples living in mainland ARMM: the Teduray, Lambangian, Dulangan Manobo and Higaonon. It covers their society, culture, economy and population, and was made with EU support.
books.overview:
This short profile reports a survey of the indigenous peoples of Maguindanao and Lanao del Sur, the mainland part of the old ARMM. It came out of IPDEV, a Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung project with EU funding on the rights of indigenous peoples in the ARMM. Its partner DEVCON ran the survey from August 2012 to February 2013 in 80 barangays across 12 municipalities.

It counted 117,189 people in 15,510 households. Of these, 110,559 were Teduray, 3,139 Lambangian and 2,905 Dulangan Manobo, along with 587 people from 17 other groups, including the Higaonon, who settled in Wao, Lanao del Sur. Together they made up about 6% of the 2 provinces' population. Sections cover households, education, housing, health, livelihoods, income and land titles.

The conclusion finds these peoples poor and marginal, with the rights promised by the Indigenous Peoples Rights Act still unrealised. It says they hold an identity distinct from both the Bangsamoro and Christian settlers. A list of the 80 barangays is included.

books.title: Beyond Paper Autonomy
books.subtitle: The Challenge in Southern Philippines
books.summary: A study of why Muslim autonomy in the southern Philippines has stayed largely 'on paper', and what real self-rule for the ARMM would require. It includes the text of the 1976 Tripoli Agreement.
books.overview:
Benedicto R. Bacani's book draws on 12 roundtable discussions on ARMM issues sponsored by the Konrad Adenauer Foundation, and gathers the views of the stakeholders who took part. It weighs autonomy as an answer to the rebellion in Mindanao, and looks at why Muslim autonomy succeeded or failed.

It ends with recommendations to make the ARMM work as a vehicle for peace and development. It also discusses federalism and other structures that could come out of the government's talks with the MILF.

The Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung published it in 2004 with the Notre Dame University College of Law in Cotabato City, and the Center for Autonomy and Governance co-sponsored the launch at the Manila Hotel on 1 September 2004.
books.note: Published with the Notre Dame University College of Law, Cotabato City.

books.title: Give Peace a Chance
books.subtitle: The Story of the GRP-MNLF Peace Talks
books.summary: An account of the peace talks between the Philippine government and the MNLF, based on the author's master's thesis at the National Defense College of the Philippines. It follows the negotiations that led to the 1996 Final Peace Agreement and public opinion around them.
books.overview:
This is an MNLF insider's account of the peace talks with the Philippine government from September 1992 to September 1996, held with the help of the Organisation of the Islamic Conference. Abraham Iribani was the MNLF's special peace emissary and chaired its secretariat for the talks. He kept detailed notes of the meetings, and the book grew out of his master's thesis at the National Defense College of the Philippines. He died in 2006, the year it was published.

The book opens with the history of the Moro wars. It then follows the exploratory talks of 1992 and 1993, the first round of formal talks in Jakarta session by session, and the mixed committee meetings, consultations and setbacks that led to the 1996 Final Peace Agreement. It also covers events that troubled the process, such as the kidnapping of 2 Spanish nuns in Sulu, fighting in Basilan and the raid on Ipil.

Soliman M. Santos Jr. wrote the foreword. The Konrad Adenauer Stiftung and the Philippine Council for Islam and Democracy published it.
books.note: Published with the Magbassa Kita Foundation.

books.title: Voices of Dissent
books.subtitle: A Postscript to the MOA-AD Decision
books.summary: A collection responding to the 2008 Supreme Court decision that struck down the GRP–MILF Memorandum of Agreement on Ancestral Domain. It gathers dissenting views on the ruling and what it meant for the peace process.
books.overview:
In 2008 the Supreme Court struck down the Memorandum of Agreement on Ancestral Domain (MOA-AD) between the government and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front. This 133-page collection gathers responses to that decision. It was published in 2009 by the Magbassa Kita Foundation with the Philippine Council for Islam and Democracy and the Konrad Adenauer Stiftung.

The book opens with 2 motions asking the Court to reconsider. Nasser Marohomsalic wrote one for the Muslim Legal Assistance Foundation, calling the Constitution a "prison wall". Soliman M. Santos Jr. wrote the other for the Consortium of Bangsamoro Civil Society and the Bangsamoro Women Solidarity Forum. Santos then comments on the decision and on the Court's denial of the motions. Further pieces come from Michael Mastura, Joaquin Bernas, Sedfrey Candelaria, Amina Rasul and Eliseo "Jun" Mercado. The book closes with reports from the Council's round-table talks on getting the peace process back on track.
books.note: Published with the Philippine Council for Islam and Democracy and Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung.

books.title: Islamic Model for Peace Education
books.summary: A peace-education resource that grounds lessons on peace in Islamic teaching, for use in Muslim communities and madaris. It has articles in English and some in Arabic.
books.overview:
This peace education manual for Muslim schools and madaris was made by the Philippine Council for Islam and Democracy (PCID) with The Asia Foundation and the Magbassa Kita Foundation, and published in Mandaluyong City in 2008. In her preface Amina Rasul explains that it grew from a 2004 visit by Dr. Asna Husin, who had worked with the ulama and madrasah teachers of Aceh in Indonesia on a peace curriculum after the armed conflict there. The PCID team included ulama and educators such as Moner Bajunaid and Hamid Barra.

The manual is a set of lessons in 7 chapters: foundations of peace in Islam, stewardship of creation and the environment, rights and responsibilities, including those of women and children, democracy, justice and good governance, conflict and its resolution, leadership in Islam, and jihad and peace. The last chapter presents jihad at several levels, including the jihad of the heart, and as an instrument of peace. Most of the text is in English, with some articles in Arabic.
books.note: Published with the Philippine Council for Islam and Democracy and the Magbassa Kita Foundation.

books.title: Noor-us Salam
books.subtitle: Women of Faith, Light of Peace: Proceedings of the Regional Conference of Women Peace Advocates, 24–27 January 2010, Davao City
books.summary: Proceedings of a 4-day regional conference in Davao City of Muslim women working for peace. It records the talks and discussions on women's roles in peacebuilding in Mindanao.
books.overview:
Noor-us Salam: Women of Faith, Light of Peace holds the proceedings of the Regional Conference of Women Peace Advocates, held at the Waterfront Insular Hotel in Davao City from 24 to 27 January 2010. The Philippine Council for Islam and Democracy (PCID) and the Magbassa Kita Foundation published the 95-page book the same year, with many colour pictures.

The conference brought together about 150 aleemat, Muslim women scholars of Islam, and women leaders from civil society. It was the start of Noorus Salam, a network of Muslim women working for peace. The idea grew from the National Ulama Summit of January 2008, where 25 aleemat asked for their own meetings on the problems of Muslim women and families. The 2 groups had already run human rights training for Muslim women since 2006, with the Commission on Human Rights. The name, "light of peace", was first used by a core group of women in Cotabato City.

The Magbassa Kita Foundation is a literacy programme begun in Sulu by the former senator Santanina Rasul. Her daughter, Amina Rasul-Bernardo, co-founded the PCID in 2002.
books.note: Published with the Magbassa Kita Foundation.

books.title: Guns, Drugs, and Extremism
books.subtitle: Bangsamoro's New Wars (Conflict Alert 2017)
books.summary: The 2017 Conflict Alert report on the causes, costs and trends of violent conflict in Muslim Mindanao from 2011 to 2016. It shows illegal guns, the drug trade and pro-ISIS extremist groups such as the Maute Group becoming major drivers of violence.
books.overview:
This is the 2017 report of Conflict Alert, International Alert's monitoring system for violence in the ARMM. It draws on police reports and news, checked with partner universities in Cotabato, Iligan and Zamboanga. Its 2 main parts compare violence in 2015 and 2016, then look at the whole period from 2011 to 2016. Data tables, the method and heat maps are in the annexes.

The report finds that 2016 saw a sharp rise in violence in every province, during the elections and the national drug war. Illegal drug incidents grew 6-fold, and drug and other illicit trades were the biggest cause of violent incidents. Gender-related violence became the second biggest cause.

Rebellion and extremist violence caused the most deaths. The report tracks the rise of groups that pledged allegiance to ISIS: the BIFF in Maguindanao, Abu Sayyaf factions in Sulu and Basilan, and the Maute Group in Lanao del Sur.

books.title: War and Identity
books.subtitle: Conflict Alert 2018
books.summary: The 2018 Conflict Alert report, written after the 2017 Marawi siege, on the threat of violent extremism in the Bangsamoro. It looks at what that threat means for the peace process and the region's future development.
books.overview:
Conflict Alert is International Alert Philippines' system for tracking violent conflict in Muslim Mindanao, begun in 2013 as the Bangsamoro Conflict Monitoring System. This edition covers 2017, the year of the Marawi siege and martial law. Its data comes from police records gathered by researchers at Notre Dame University in Cotabato City, Western Mindanao State University and MSU-Iligan Institute of Technology, checked by local validation groups in each area.

The report looks at how often conflict occurred, its human cost and its causes, then turns to violent extremism, the shadow economy of drugs, guns and gambling, violence against women and children, and urban conflict. It found that 2017 had fewer violent incidents than 2016 but far more deaths. Rebellion by the MNLF, MILF and communist rebels nearly disappeared, while extremist violence, clashes over religious identity and urban violence rose.

The report weighs 2 explanations for Marawi: that it marked a new kind of extremism, or that many fighters came from older secessionist struggles and switched allegiance to ISIS.

books.title: War Makes States
books.subtitle: Conflict Alert 2019
books.summary: The 2019 Conflict Alert report on the fall in violent incidents in Muslim Mindanao after the Marawi war, even as extremist violence continued. Its title borrows Charles Tilly's line that war makes states, as the BARMM was being set up.
books.overview:
Conflict Alert is International Alert's system for tracking violent conflict in the Bangsamoro, built with partner universities, the police and local validation groups. This 2019 report covers its 8th year of data, from 2011 to 2018, and was edited by Liezl Bugtay, Nikki Philline de la Rosa and Judy Gulane. It was funded by the World Bank and the Australian government.

It counts 2,910 violent incidents in 2018, a 30% drop from 4,140 in 2017. Deaths also fell. The report gives martial law, with more police and military checkpoints, as the most likely reason. Chapters cover incidents by province, the human cost, causes of conflict, gender-based violence, land conflict in the Iranun corridor, timing and weapons.

It warns that the region is "not out of the woods yet". Extremist violence had become the leading cause of conflict deaths since 2016, and violence tied to the transition was growing. The title quotes the sociologist Charles Tilly, and one section looks at how war has shaped the building of the state in Muslim Mindanao.

books.title: Enduring Wars
books.subtitle: Conflict Alert 2020
books.summary: The 2020 Conflict Alert report, analysing conflict data and trends in the Bangsamoro from 2011 to 2019. It tracks how long-running clan, political, criminal and extremist violence continued into the first year of the BARMM.
books.overview:
Conflict Alert is a conflict monitoring system run by the Philippines programme of International Alert. It tracks violent incidents, their causes and their human cost down to the village level. This edition covers 2019, the year the BARMM was created, and brings the dataset to 9 years. It was funded by the World Bank and the Australian Government, with Western Mindanao State University and Notre Dame University as partners.

The report finds that violence fell for the third year in a row, to 2,655 incidents, 9% fewer than in 2018. Lanao del Sur went the other way: incidents rose 29% and deaths 26%. Extremist incidents in Basilan dropped by 62%. Illegal drugs and illicit guns were the leading single causes of violence, and deaths from clan feuds rose 53% to 107.

Chapters cover the region in 2019, the method, conflict by province, causes and deaths. A section on flashpoints looks at rising clan feuds, resource conflicts, violent extremism, the anti-drug campaign and tensions over the rebuilding of Marawi.

books.title: Rebellion, Political Violence and Shadow Crimes in the Bangsamoro
books.subtitle: The Bangsamoro Conflict Monitoring System (BCMS), 2011–2013
books.summary: The first report from the Bangsamoro Conflict Monitoring System, built with police data and university partners. It maps violent incidents in the ARMM from 2011 to 2013 and links them to rebellion, clan feuds, politics and illicit economies.
books.overview:
This report presents the first 3 years of data from the Bangsamoro Conflict Monitoring System, set up by International Alert with World Bank funding. It draws on Philippine National Police reports and news, worked through with Mindanao State University, Western Mindanao State University and local validation groups.

It maps violence by province, cause and time of year from 2011 to 2013. Shadow economies such as guns, drugs and kidnapping caused 27% of incidents. Political violence, clan feuds and crimes by private armed groups made up much of the rest. Violence rose around elections, in the lean months before harvest and at the start of the school year.

The report finds that rebellion caused fewer incidents but more deaths than other causes. Basilan had the most violence per person, and Sulu had few incidents but many deaths. It warns that a peace agreement alone will not end violence in the region.

books.title: Compromising on Autonomy
books.subtitle: Mindanao in Transition (Accord issue 6)
books.summary: An issue of the Accord series on the negotiations between the Philippine government and the MNLF that led to the 1996 'Final Peace Agreement'. Published with MSU General Santos and Notre Dame University, it carries essays, interviews, profiles and the key texts of the agreements.
books.overview:
Issue 6 of Accord, the peace process series of the London-based Conciliation Resources, looks at the 1996 Final Peace Agreement between the Philippine government and the Moro National Liberation Front. That deal ended 24 years of war after every earlier attempt at a settlement had failed, though carrying it out did not end the violence. The issue was edited by Mara Stankovitch, with contributors including Rufa Cagoco-Guiam, Carolyn Arguillas, Macapado Muslim, Soliman Santos Jr. and Eric Gutierrez.

The 1999 articles cover the agreement itself, Mindanao as a "land of promise", Islamic diplomacy, the constituency for Moro autonomy, civil society's part in the process and the politics of transition. There are interviews with the MILF's Mohagher Iqbal and with Ramon Moambing on the Lumad, along with key texts, a chronology, profiles and further reading.

In 2003 a supplement, prepared with the MSU Centre for Peace Studies, added articles on the talks and fighting with the Moro Islamic Liberation Front and on civil society initiatives such as local monitoring teams and "spaces for peace".

books.title: Women's Voices in the Bangsamoro
books.subtitle: Experiences and Expectations in Conflict and Peace
books.summary: First-person stories of Moro and Teduray women: fighters, wives of combatants, women caught between armies, and peace advocates. It was made jointly by 3 Bangsamoro women's organisations and Conciliation Resources.
books.overview:
This book gathers first-person stories from women of the Bangsamoro: Moro, Lumad and settler. It was made by Nisa Ul Haqq Fi Bangsamoro, UnYPhil-Women and the Teduray Lambangian Women's Organisation with Conciliation Resources, and published in March 2016 with British government funding.

The stories are grouped in 5 parts: women on the frontline of armed conflict, women in the families of fighters, women caught in between and fleeing conflict, women who chose peace and faced their own biases, and daily life beyond the conflict. Among them is Hadja Aziza Tabayag, who joined the MNLF and became a commander after her husband and 4 sons were killed in 1973, and Elsie Benito Travilla, a Teduray woman who resisted extortion and land grabbing in South Upi.

A closing section draws out the roles women played: heads of family, sources of hope, fighters, leaders and peacebuilders. It came out of a wider project, begun in 2013, to secure women's meaningful participation in the Bangsamoro under the 2014 peace agreement.
books.note: Published with Nisa Ul Haqq Fi Bangsamoro, UnYPhil-Women and the Teduray Lambangian Women’s Organization.

books.title: Human Development for Peace and Prosperity in the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao
books.summary: A World Bank study of health, education and social services in the ARMM, the country's poorest region. It argues that better human development is needed for peace and growth in Muslim Mindanao.
books.overview:
This World Bank study, by Teresa J. Ho, sets out the state of human development in the ARMM in 2003. It asks why outcomes were so poor, and how far public and private services eased or worsened them.

The study names 3 main causes of the region's large gaps in basic education and health: extreme poverty, conflict and historical disadvantage. It looks in depth at the education sector, the health system and social protection. It asks why the ARMM lagged other regions, and what could be changed with the money available and under the political and social conditions of the time.

It ends with recommendations on public spending levels and on actions for each sector.

books.title: Joint Needs Assessment for Reconstruction and Development of Conflict-Affected Areas in Mindanao
books.subtitle: Integrative Report, Volume 1
books.summary: The main report of a large needs assessment of conflict-affected areas of Mindanao, made jointly with the government, international agencies and local stakeholders. It sets out what reconstruction and development would need after a peace agreement with the MILF, and led to the Mindanao Trust Fund.
books.overview:
This is the main report of a needs assessment of conflict-affected areas in Mindanao. The World Bank led it with the Philippine government, other donors, UN agencies and local stakeholders, including the Bangsamoro Development Agency. Its results were meant to shape a reconstruction programme funded through a multi-donor Mindanao Trust Fund.

The team reviewed existing studies, held consultations in Davao City and Manila, and then visited sample municipalities for workshops, interviews and focus groups. The report opens with a history of the conflict and the social situation of the region.

Its core chapters set out needs in 4 sectors: human development, rural development, finance and private sector development, and local governance. It also covers displaced people, gender, the environment and land tenure. The last chapters give priorities, the role of government, risks and the money needed.
books.note: Prepared with the Government of the Philippines, the Bangsamoro Development Agency and the international funding agencies.

books.title: Making Education Spending Count for the Children of the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM)
books.subtitle: Public Expenditure and Institutional Review for ARMM
books.summary: A review of how public money for basic education is spent and managed in the ARMM, where learning outcomes are the lowest in the country. It recommends ways to make that spending reach schools and children.
books.overview:
This public expenditure and institutional review was made at the request of ARMM Regional Governor Mujiv Hataman, as a joint report of the World Bank and Australia's foreign affairs department. It asks how money for basic education in the ARMM was planned, budgeted and spent, and why results were so poor. A schools survey by the Consortium of Bangsamoro Civil Society, with over 90 enumerators, made surprise visits to schools across the region.

The report sets out the region's history and education record, then its budget system, its spending on teachers, operating funds, textbooks and classrooms, and the problems of getting that money to schools. In 2011–12 only 23% of Grade 1 pupils reached Grade 6, against 73.5% nationally. The survey found many schools closed, with teacher absence of about 31% and pupil absence of 29%, worst in Lanao del Sur. The authors trace these problems to a fragmented, poorly linked budget system they call the ARMM "PEM syndrome".

It ends with an action plan on ghost teachers, payroll, school operating funds and accountability, and lessons for the coming Bangsamoro.

books.title: Unlocking the Potential of the Bangsamoro People through the Alternative Learning System
books.summary: A World Bank report on the Alternative Learning System, the second-chance education programme for out-of-school youth and adults, in the Bangsamoro region. It looks at who needs it and how the new BARMM can expand and improve it.
books.overview:
This World Bank report, dated October 2019, studies the Alternative Learning System (ALS) in the new BARMM. ALS is the Department of Education's second-chance programme for out-of-school youth and adults. Earlier World Bank evaluations of ALS had not covered the region, and this one was meant to give the new Bangsamoro government evidence for reform.

It notes that only 1 in 10 BARMM pupils who started primary school finished junior high school on time, and that close to 45% of people aged 16 to 30 were out of school, double the national rate. In 2018 only 5% of them took part in ALS, against 13% nationally. Learners had weaker reading, maths and socioemotional skills, and there was 1 ALS teacher for every 1,800 out-of-school youth and adults, the highest ratio of any region.

Chapters cover the sector, the learners, programme delivery and its bottlenecks, and policy recommendations. These include better training for ALS teachers, better outreach and closer supervision to end irregular practices.

books.title: The Transition to Universal Health Coverage in BARMM
books.subtitle: Delivering and Financing Health Services in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao
books.summary: A long study of how health services are delivered and paid for in the BARMM as the region takes up the national Universal Health Care law. It maps gaps in facilities, staff and financing and sets out options for the new regional Ministry of Health.
books.overview:
This World Bank report assesses how health care is paid for and delivered in the Bangsamoro region. The work began while the region was still the ARMM. The authors note that this timing let them hand their evidence to the new BARMM leaders during the transition, as the national Universal Health Care Law of 2019 also took effect.

It has 9 chapters. They cover the national health system, the region's history and politics, health financing, a 2019 household survey on access to basic health services, how ready primary care facilities are, the immunisation programme, public financial management, and a proposed structure for the regional Ministry of Health. Annexes give survey details and the reasoning for the proposed structure.

One finding is that health funding under the ARMM was badly fragmented. Separate funding streams each had their own planning and reporting rules, and national appropriations provided up to 65% of the money.

books.title: Beyond the Numbers
books.subtitle: Sustaining Poverty Reduction in BARMM (Philippines Economic Update, June 2024)
books.summary: An edition of the World Bank's Philippines Economic Update whose special focus is poverty in the BARMM. It looks at how poverty in the region fell and what is needed to keep it falling.
books.overview:
This edition of the World Bank's Philippines Economic Update has 3 parts. Parts 1 and 2 cover the national economy and its outlook. Part 3 is a special study of poverty in the BARMM between 2018 and 2021.

It finds that poverty in the region fell by 24.6 percentage points over that time, against the national trend and during the pandemic. The report links the fall to the peace that came with the Bangsamoro Organic Law and to more public funds. Higher wages from a shift out of farming explain nearly 40% of the drop. Private and government transfers explain about half.

The BARMM is still the poorest region. It holds 4% of the country's people but 8% of its poor, and 36% of its people are near-poor. The report points to gaps in water, electricity and access to markets, and suggests ways to keep poverty falling.

books.title: Philippine Human Development Report 2005
books.subtitle: Peace, Human Security and Human Development in the Philippines
books.summary: The 2005 national human development report, devoted to the costs of armed conflict in the Philippines, including the Moro conflict and the communist insurgency. It treats human security as a precondition of human development and examines prejudice against Muslims as a driver of conflict.
books.overview:
The 5th Philippine Human Development Report turns from economics to armed conflict. It looks at the causes and costs of the communist and Moro insurgencies, why government policy has failed to end them, and how peace efforts could be strengthened. The Human Development Network prepared it with UNDP and New Zealand aid. Emmanuel de Dios and Soliman Santos Jr. wrote the main chapter, drawing on commissioned papers, case studies, workshops including one at MSU General Santos, and a national opinion poll.

Among its findings: 91% of provinces were hit by armed conflict between 1986 and 2004. The Mindanao conflict cost an estimated P5 billion to P10 billion a year from 1975 to 2002. Between one-fifth and one-third of the major Muslim groups now live outside their ancestral homelands. Polls showed latent anti-Muslim bias among 33% to 39% of Filipinos. Poverty rates alone did not predict where fighting happened, but gaps in water, power and schooling did.

The report calls for a common peace framework, a national peace policy set in law, and a national constituency for peace.
books.note: Published with the UN Development Programme.

books.title: The Contested Corners of Asia
books.subtitle: Subnational Conflict and International Development Assistance: The Case of Mindanao, Philippines
books.summary: The Mindanao case study of a multi-country Asia Foundation research project on aid in long-running subnational conflicts. Using field research and a perception survey by Social Weather Stations, it asks whether development aid in conflict areas of Mindanao has helped or hurt peace.
books.overview:
Fermin Adriano and Thomas Parks wrote this Mindanao report for The Asia Foundation's study of aid in long-running conflicts in Asian border regions. It was co-financed by the World Bank and UK Aid. It asks whether development aid to the conflict areas of Mindanao has helped the move from instability to peace.

The research team drew on a household perceptions survey with Social Weather Stations, case studies of municipalities, many key informant interviews, and official and violence data. They looked at communities rather than single projects. Chapters cover the history of the Moro conflict, aid strategies of selected donors, how local elites and armed groups shape aid at community level, and how aid could do more.

The report finds that despite large amounts of aid for more than a decade, the conflict had not improved. It does not blame poorly designed programmes. It argues that the conflict is so entrenched that peace may take decades, far longer than aid project cycles, and that weak monitoring makes it hard to know what works.

books.title: Bangsamoro Development Plan
books.subtitle: Integrative Report
books.summary: The 6-year development plan for the Bangsamoro drawn up by the MILF through the BDA, with government and donor support, under the Framework Agreement on the Bangsamoro. It covers the history of the conflict, community consultations and plans for each sector, in 15 chapters.
books.overview:
The Bangsamoro Development Plan Integrative Report opens with messages from MILF Chairman Al-Haj Murad Ebrahim and BDA Chairman Saffrullah M. Dipatuan. The first chapters give a short history of the Bangsamoro struggle and peace process, explain how the plan was made, and assess the region's development gaps and opportunities.

Chapter 5, "Clamor from the Ground", reports on Community Visioning Exercises that the Bangsamoro Development Agency held to learn people's needs and grievances. Later chapters set out a strategy and sector plans for 6 themes: economy and livelihood, infrastructure, social services, environment and natural resources, culture and identity, and governance.

The last chapters propose how to carry out and pay for the plan, name the risks and ways to reduce them, and set up a results-based monitoring and evaluation system. Annexes list priority programmes, the poorest provinces and municipalities, and the cultural diversity of the Bangsamoro.

books.title: Transitional Justice and Reconciliation in and beyond the Bangsamoro
books.summary: A research study and resource guide from IID's Bangsamoro Transformative Justice Initiatives project, 2017 to 2019. It explains transitional justice, dealing with the past and reconciliation, and records community stories of survival and truth-telling.
books.overview:
This study comes from the Initiatives for International Dialogue's Bangsamoro Transformative Justice Initiatives project, 2017 to 2019. Over 2 years the team listened to Moro, indigenous and settler survivors of violence in Mindanao. The work built on the Transitional Justice and Reconciliation Commission of the Bangsamoro peace process.

The book has 4 parts. Part 1 sets out the research and its Mindanao context. Part 2 reviews ideas of transitional justice, reconciliation and restorative justice from around the world. Part 3 gives 5 community case studies, including stories from a Moro child of war, the Ilaga, Mt. Firis and post-war Marawi, and looks at indigenous, Moro and Christian sources of justice.

Part 4 analyses the findings and proposes a framework that roots community-based restorative justice in dealing with the past. It ends with policy recommendations for government, culture, education and the security sector.

books.title: Land Rights, Displacement, and Transitional Justice in the Bangsamoro
books.subtitle: Insights from Household-level Mapping in Marawi City and Maguindanao
books.summary: A research report on land loss and displacement in Marawi City and Maguindanao, based on household-level mapping. It argues that land dispossession is a root cause of conflict in the Bangsamoro that transitional justice must address.
books.overview:
This summary report starts from the view that land dispossession is a root cause of conflict in the Bangsamoro, past and present. From late 2021 to mid-2022, research teams mapped land and displacement with families in Marawi City and in South Upi and the Firis Complex in Maguindanao. The lead researcher was Maria Carmen "Ica" Fernandez of the University of Cambridge, working with the Initiatives for International Dialogue, MSU Marawi, the Kalimudan sa Ranao Foundation, UNYPAD, Timuay Justice and Governance and a Tëduray-Lambangian women's group.

In Marawi the teams worked with displaced families in shelters, imams of 42 mosques in the most affected area, traders from the old padian market and one neighbourhood fighting land cases. In Maguindanao they mapped homes and farm lots in 3 sites with recurring land violence, among Tëduray-Lambangian, Maguindanaon and settler residents.

The report finds that land laws imported from the West a century ago still harm displaced Moro and indigenous peoples. It calls for a single land framework for the Bangsamoro, built on reliable data that records both formal titles and customary claims, with separate recommendations for Marawi and Maguindanao.
books.note: Published with UNYPAD, Timuay Justice and Governance, the Teduray-Lambangian Women’s Organization, Kalimudan sa Ranao Foundation, MSU Marawi and the University of Cambridge.

books.title: In War, the Real Enemy Is War Itself
books.summary: Reflections by the Oblate parish priest of Pikit, Cotabato, a town repeatedly caught in fighting between the army and the MILF. Drawing on what war did to Muslim and Christian villagers there, it argues that war itself is the enemy.
books.overview:
Father Roberto Layson, a Filipino Oblate priest, was parish priest of Pikit in Cotabato, a town caught again and again in fighting between the army and the MILF. In his first 6 years there, he wrote later, 4 wars brought havoc and great suffering to thousands of civilians, Muslim and Christian. This short book of 68 pages, published in 2003 by the Initiatives for International Dialogue, records the images of those wars and draws the lesson in its title: the real enemy in war is war itself.

Layson received the Pax Christi International Peace Award in 2002 for building a culture of peace among Christians, Muslims and indigenous people in a conflict area. His 2011 book Fields of Hope was a follow-up. He said the first book showed the images of war, while the second aimed to bring hope.

books.title: Moving Beyond
books.subtitle: Towards Transitional Justice in the Bangsamoro Peace Process
books.summary: The first collection on transitional justice in the Bangsamoro, launched in Davao City in July 2014. It explains the concept, draws lessons from other countries, and looks at truth, justice, reparation and reconciliation in Central Mindanao.
books.overview:
forumZFD, a German peace organisation working in Mindanao since 2008, published this collection in Davao City in 2014, with funding from the German development ministry. The editorial team was Venus Betita, Manuel Domes, Daniel Jaeger, Lotte Kirch and Jeremy Simons. Forewords come from Cardinal Orlando Quevedo, Raissa Jajurie and Timuay Santos Unsad.

The book has 3 parts. The first explains transitional justice as an evolving idea, with an essay on its foundations by Jasmina Brankovic and Hugo van der Merwe and one on Latin America by Rosario Figari Layús. The second draws lessons from other places, including Galuh Wandita's notes from Aceh. The third turns to the Bangsamoro: Rosa Cordillera Castillo on truth, justice, reparation and reconciliation in Central Mindanao, Marian Pastor Roces, and Jurma Tikmasan on the island provinces of Western Mindanao.

In his foreword, Cardinal Quevedo reads the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro itself as an expression of transitional justice.

books.title: Transitional Justice in the Bangsamoro
books.subtitle: What's Next?
books.summary: A follow-up to a 2023 conference in which transitional justice experts and practitioners reflect on what has been done on justice and reconciliation in the Bangsamoro. It sets out what is still needed in the BARMM.
books.overview:
This 2024 publication from forumZFD (now Pro Peace) follows a conference of the same name that it held with GIZ's Civil Peace Service on 7 to 9 February 2023. About 200 people from government, civil society, communities and the international field took part. The book makes the results available to practitioners and asks experts what has been done for justice and reconciliation in the Bangsamoro and what is still needed.

It opens with messages from Mohagher Iqbal of the MILF and Carlito Galvez Jr. of the peace adviser's office. Karlos Manlupig then retells the 1971 massacre at the mosque of Manili in Carmen, North Cotabato, through its survivors and their children. Yasmira Moner looks at how little of the 2016 Transitional Justice and Reconciliation Commission report, with its more than 90 recommendations, has been carried out.

Further essays, by Cecilia Jimenez-Damary, Bai Shaima Baraguir and Rosa Cordillera Castillo, Kriselle Marie Aquino, and Abel Moya and Elnathan Ermac, cover local ownership, reparations, the Bangsamoro Human Rights Commission and the interfaith group Pakigdait in Kauswagan.
books.note: Published with the GIZ Civil Peace Service.

books.title: Mapagpakamalinawon
books.subtitle: A Reader for the Mindanawon Peace Advocate
books.summary: A reader for peace workers on Mindanao's history, ethnic relations and Muslim–Christian relations. It was written for Mindanao peace advocates and co-published with Catholic Relief Services.
books.overview:
Mapagpakamalinawon is a reader for people working for peace in Mindanao. It was put together by Karl M. Gaspar, Elpidio A. Lapad and Ailynne J. Maravillas and published by the Alternate Forum for Research in Mindanao. It runs to nearly 300 pages, and editions also appeared in Cebuano and Filipino.

The book tells the stories of ordinary people and communities working to keep unity and peaceful coexistence alive in Mindanao. They try to carve out "oases of peace" on an island of strife. A Mindanao annotated bibliography reads these stories as signs that Mindanawons are turning away from violence and seeking peaceful solutions.
books.note: Published with Catholic Relief Services Philippines.

books.title: In Defense of and Thinking beyond the GRP-MILF MOA-AD
books.subtitle: A Peace Advocate's Essays on the Controversial Memorandum of Agreement on Ancestral Domain
books.summary: Essays by a peace advocate and lawyer defending the 2008 Memorandum of Agreement on Ancestral Domain, which the Supreme Court struck down. They also propose ways forward for the GRP–MILF talks after its collapse.
books.overview:
Soliman M. Santos Jr., a lawyer and peace advocate, gathers his essays on the Memorandum of Agreement on Ancestral Domain between the government and the MILF. The agreement was due to be signed on 5 August 2008 but was stopped, and the Supreme Court later struck it down. The earliest essay is dated that same day.

The book is a compilation rather than a single argument. Some essays defend the agreement against its critics. Others look past it to what the talks should do next. In one paper Santos proposed to "leap-frog" over the failed agreement and move straight to negotiating a comprehensive compact.

The Alternate Forum for Research in Mindanao published the book in Davao City and launched it with the Mindanao Peoples' Caucus on 15 July 2011.

books.title: Troubled Odyssey
books.subtitle: The GRP-MILF Peace Process
books.summary: A long account of the talks between the government and the MILF, by a veteran Cotabato journalist who followed them from the start.
books.overview:
Patricio P. Diaz was a veteran Cotabato journalist and a long-time commentator on Muslim autonomy. This book is his detailed account of the long and difficult peace talks between the Government of the Philippines and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front. He wrote that he began it in October 2009 and finished in June 2011, a year later than planned.

Diaz frames the search for a political solution to the Moro problem as grounded in the Bangsamoro right to self-determination. At the launch in Davao City on 8 July 2011, he said Moro leaders had to be clear about what kind of autonomy would solve their problem, and warned that they would never attain it if they stayed divided.
